Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. With our current account deficit aggravating our foreign exchange position, we now find that the capital outflow from Canada continues at alarming rates. The figures in the March, 1978, Bank of Canada review show that in 1976 unidentified capital outflows were $3.4 billion and in 1977 they were $3.2 billion compared to, say, three years ago when they were only $600 million. Will the Minister of Finance indicate if they have reviewed these figures to determine the cause of this type of outflow? If so, what can he report to the House?

Mr. Speaker, this question was asked some days ago by the hon. member's seatmate. We have reviewed these figures. There is nothing special to report. I have prepared a letter for the hon. member's seatmate and I will send a copy of it to the hon. member for York-Simcoe in order that he will have a lengthy explanation.

The Minister of Finance has indicated there is nothing unusual about the $6 billion of unidentified capital outflows. Will he indicate whether consideration has been given to contingency plans in order to relieve the situation with regard to our foreign exchange position? If so, will he indicate what those contingency plans are?
Oral Questions
There is nothing special that I can add at this time on the exchange rate and the policies that the government has been following. I gave plenty of explanation in my budget speech.

Is the Minister of Finance aware that the Department of Justice has drafted legislation which provides for a limitation on capital outflows by residents of Canada, restricting them in any year to $600 of capital outflow? Is he aware of that legislation being drafted in the Department of Justice? Will he indicate who requested it and what its purpose is?
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I am aware of no such legislation and the government has no intention of introducing capital controls in Canada.

subsubtopic: PROSECUTION OF MEMBERS COMMITTING ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Solicitor General. It arises from recent testimony before the McDonald commission which has shown that members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police

took part in illegal activities for which they could be prosecuted under the Criminal Code. The Solicitor General is quoted in today's Globe and Mail as saying he is not planning to take any action in connection with these breaches of the Criminal Code. Can the minister tell us why he does not intend to take action against those who broke the law of Canada?

subsubtopic: PROSECUTION OF MEMBERS COMMITTING ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has undoubtedly read the terms of reference of the McDonald commission. They include power to inquire into procedures which might not have been authorized by specific legal provisions. The evidence in the past week has shown-if this is what the hon. member is referring to-that there have been what are called surreptitious entries. A legal opinion has been forthcoming from the Department of Justice to the effect that these procedures are legal. There is a decided opinion with reference to their legality, and I wish the evidence were completely adduced before the commission so that the inquiry, which is proceeding apace, would be able to make a judgment and bring in its own recommendations.

subsubtopic: PROSECUTION OF MEMBERS COMMITTING ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext: In view of the expectation that the McDonald commission will not be reporting until 1980 or 1981, and that in the minds of the Canadian people justice delayed is justice denied, and since the royal commission will be examining the procedures followed by the RCMP in carrying out their duties-while what we are talking about, in effect, has to do with the illegal actions of individuals-can the minister tell us what specific steps he and his department plan to take now that he is aware of specific criminal actions on the part of certain members of the RCMP?

subsubtopic: PROSECUTION OF MEMBERS COMMITTING ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext: With reference to the specific illegal acts which the hon. member has mentioned, those acts were referred to the attorneys general of the provinces in which they were allegedly perpetrated. The inquiry is continuing to deal with other matters, such as the procedures followed. The hon. member has cited 1980 or 1981 as the termination date for the inquiry. That is a judgment which a reporter has made, it is not my judgment. Hopefully, the commission will be reporting post-haste-

subsubtopic: PROSECUTION OF MEMBERS COMMITTING ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext: Post-haste?

subsubtopic: PROSECUTION OF MEMBERS COMMITTING ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext: -to this House. Further, as I have said before, the commission can make interim reports as it sees fit.

subsubtopic: PROSECUTION OF MEMBERS COMMITTING ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is absolutely appalling that the chief law officer of the nation should give responses such as we have heard this afternoon. Can he tell this House and the people why any Canadian should respect the rule of law in this country when the government has decided it may be inoperative at any time the circumstances suit it?

subtopic: DELAY IN INFORMING MCDONALD INQUIRY OF ILLEGAL ACTS
DELAY IN INFORMING MCDONALD INQUIRY OF ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Solicitor General. The press report indicates that the government knew last September
April 25, 1978

about several hundred entries made without warrants. I refer the Solicitor General to the commitment of his predecessor to refer to the commissioners of the McDonald commission and to law enforcement agencies, not evidence of alleged illegalities but, to quote the minister's immediate predecessor, "any alleged breach of Canadian laws"-which is a far different thing.
Can the Solicitor General tell the House why, if his predecessor knew last September, it was not until last week that the McDonald commission was informed of this type of activity in direct evidence, when a clear commitment was made in this House on October 28 by the minister's predecessor to inform immediately the commission and other law enforcement agencies of any alleged breach of Canadian laws?

subtopic: DELAY IN INFORMING MCDONALD INQUIRY OF ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman has read the terms of reference, he will know that the commission has jurisdiction to study procedures, as I indicated to the hon. gentleman from Nickel Belt. I indicated in that interview that indeed there was knowledge of the procedure of surreptitious entries. There was no indication by me that there was knowledge of 400 specific events, as was the evidence last week. However, that evidence, of necessity-

subtopic: DELAY IN INFORMING MCDONALD INQUIRY OF ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext: You were quoted.

subtopic: DELAY IN INFORMING MCDONALD INQUIRY OF ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext:
I was not quoted. Of necessity the evidence relating to surreptitious entries was made known to me and my predecessor some time before, but in accordance with the procedures of the McDonald inquiry such evidence was prepared so that it could be led by my solicitors before that commission.
I would like to indicate to the hon. gentleman that it is an indication of the excellent co-operation that there is presently, and has been, between the RCMP, my department and the commission that there is a proper scheduling of the evidence and the presentation of that evidence before the commission. The hon. gentleman will understand that evidence relating to procedures cannot all be introduced before the commission on the same day.

subtopic: DELAY IN INFORMING MCDONALD INQUIRY OF ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue is not the co-operation that exists; the issue is the competence and responsibility of the minister of the day and the present minister. Can the Solicitor General indicate to this House whether it is his view that the present terms of reference enable the McDonald commission to advise that charges be laid against whomever, because on reading the terms of reference it is certainly not clear to me nor, I presume, to others that any such power exists within those terms of reference?
While the minister is answering that, perhaps he would also tell the House the difference between an alleged culpable act committed one day before the McDonald commission was constituted, and a similar culpable act one day after; because it is very clear in the press story-unless it is incorrect-that the Solicitor General distinguishes clearly between any activity up to the moment the McDonald commission was constituted and any activity which occurred after that constitution.
Oral Questions

subtopic: DELAY IN INFORMING MCDONALD INQUIRY OF ILLEGAL ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the hon. gentleman is making distinctions where distinctions do not appear. What I did say was that if an illegal activity is made known to me, and that illegal activity is expressly contrary to policy directives which I have issued or which my predecessor may have issued, that activity will be the subject of possible prosecution. I wish to advise the hon. gentleman that it is the policy of the commissioner of the RCMP that any illegal activity which comes to his attention is referred immediately to the attorney general of the province concerned, who has responsibility for the administration of justice.
With reference to the other distinction which the hon. gentleman wishes to make regarding the terms of reference, I would like to take note of his questions because they deal with a very precise interpretation. I will report to the hon. gentleman.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. In a recent statement in

Alberta, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce stated with reference to the Canadian dollar:
I don't believe it is any advantage to advocate it should be above 90 cents,
He also suggested that the Canadian dollar should be renamed Beaver. Can the Minister of Finance say whether that is government policy, or was the minister flying a kite to assess public acceptance of the fact that the Canadian dollar will never recover?

Mr. Speaker, the policy of the government regarding the dollar is well known. I think the suggestion of calling it Beaver is as original as the one made by the Secretary of the Treasury of the United States that we could perhaps call it Maple Leaf.

The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce also said "there is no rhyme nor reason why it should be equal" to the U.S. dollar, and then mentioned the advantages of the devalued dollar. Has the government calculated the adverse effects which the devalued Canadian dollar has on the economy?

Mr. Speaker, there are some positive and some negative aspects to the floating dollar. This is the policy which the government has been following for years. Of course, it is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to speak about the advantages because a weaker dollar is very good for the export business.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased on this occasion to present this motion before the House on behalf of my party. I believe the subject matter of the motion is very timely.
It will give the House an opportunity to examine the Trudeau government's record in the important area of transportation. It will give the House an opportunity to examine the reliability of the Liberal government in fulfilling the election promises of 1974. It will give us an opportunity to assess and analyse the effectiveness and the manner in which the current minister is handling the day to day issues which arise. It will provide hon. members an opportunity to consider some new initiatives and new directions in the formulation of goals, objectives, and priorities for a national transportation policy in Canada into the twenty-first century. It will also give us an opportunity to discuss how we might be able to execute such policy. Perhaps what is more important is that as we now head into another election campaign there is no question in the minds of many people that Canadians will again, in all probability, be bombarded with another assortment of transporta-
Transportation
tion goodies, which the Liberals have no intention of implementing even if they were elected.
Hear, hear!

As a matter of fact that process is well on its way right now, Mr. Speaker. Whole promises are being reactivated. So-called new commitments are being introduced, along with so-called new promises, all of which are politically motivated. I am glad the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is in the House because he is the master of political motivation. I am sure that Canadians this time around will look upon that kind of benevolence and that kind of charity with much disdain.
Let us take a look at some of the highlights of the 1974 election campaign commitments. On June 19, 1974, the man who once proclaimed that Canada's transportation policy was in a mess and who got his reward in the other place, said this in a press release-
What about the future?
Yes, we will get to the future, but we have to review the past before we do that.
Hear, hear!
Order, please. Will the hon. member please address the Chair.

Mr. Speaker, I will certainly abide by your ruling. I would never insult the Chair, and you know that, sir.
The important issue in the next election campaign which will be the Trudeau government's record, and particularly its record with respect to transportation policy-
He does not want to run on his record.

In a June 19, 1974, press release it was reported:
Transport Minister Jean Marchand today announced sweeping changes in the institutional structures which manage Canadian transportation, a radical departure from past transportation philosophy and a comprehensive set of new transportation programs for Canada. "These changes and these programs are going to move Canada toward world leadership in the use and construction of passenger and freight transportation systems. We are reaching for world leadership in quality equipment and systems," Mr. Marchand said.
That was June, 1974, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member across the way has a short memory. He forgets about these commitments, as do most members across the way, including the Minister of Transport. These commitments were made by a former minister of transport. Let us bear in mind that this is the man who suggested that transportation systems were in a mess. I submit to you, sir, that if clearing up the so-called mess was contingent upon the fulfilment of that lofty statement, then one can only conclude that the mess has become worse.
What radical departure from past transportation philosophy have we seen or heard? What new set of comprehensive transportation programs or proposals have we seen? What

April 25, 1978
Transportation
kind of world leadership has been displayed by this government? The fact of the matter is none. Those who are involved in the transportation industry would probably not agree that our systems were all that bad. If there ever was a mess in the transportation industry in Canada, that mess was in the transportation minister's office. I have every reason to believe there has been very little improvement since that infamous statement was made. It is quite obvious the condition still exists.
Let us look at some samples, Mr. Speaker, first of all respecting urban transportation. On June 17, 1974, there was an announcement that some $290 million would be provided in the form of financial aid for urban transportation systems. That never got off the ground. The provinces took the commitment as a good word. They went to work, developed programs, and perhaps even committed the expenditure of those funds.
On February 17, 1977, the then minister of finance, Mr. Macdonald, announced cancellation of the program due to fiscal restraint. Lie cancelled it in the same city in which it had been announced three years earlier. They used fiscal restraint as an excuse, but it is very interesting to note that inflation was running at something like 11 Vi per cent during the election campaign of 1974. Restraint was not much of an issue at that time.
When Mr. Macdonald announced cancellation of the program, inflation was running in the order of 8 per cent. It is therefore obvious that the program was announced for political expediency and for political gain. There is no question about that. Even Liberal members of parliament could not stomach the government's about-face. Many of them spoke out on the matter, including the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Phil-brook), the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin), the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette), the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo), the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp), and the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson). All expressed shock and dismay at the blatancy of the government reneging on what was considered to be a formal and honest commitment. They did garner some votes however.
The minister of transportation in the province of Ontario described it as one of the most unresponsive and disappointing transporation programs put forward by the federal government in years. He stated that over the past three years the federal government indicated it would be willing to support the development of urban public transportation. This was not a casual or "maybe" commitment. They were public statements of the federal government's intent to give full support to this important program. What we have is a broken promise. It can be described as nothing else.
What about ferry service? The Liberal campaign document described that we would have a comprehensive new policy for expanding assistance to the ferry service in Canada. What was the result? A dramatic increase in tolls in our ferry system, reaching almost 70 per cent in the province of British
[Mr. Mazankowski.l
Columbia. It almost caused the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) to leave the cabinet.
What about ports? We were to have a comprehensive program to improve railway access to western ports and to Vancouver. This was to be launched immediately. As a matter of fact this launching was to have taken place in 1973 at the WEOC conference in Calgary. That launching is still sputtering. We were to have had new legislation to provide greater autonomy to the port authorities. Bill C-6 which was introduced contravenes that philosophy and principle.
What about freight rates? This is a dandy. It was the major priority of the Liberal government in the election campaign of 1974. They said this:
The third major priority of these new transportation policies is the removal of regional inequities in freight rates. Mr. Marchand said it has been demonstrated over the past six years that the principle of competition on which Canadian freight rates has been based, that is, competition between different modes of transport supposedly resulting in fair and low rates, has not worked for many areas in Canada. The Liberal government will adopt the principle of consistent and equitable pricing of freight rates rather than the old "what the traffic will bear" principle. This will be a dramatic change-and the government intends to monitor the implementation very carefully to cushion shippers and carriers.
The fact is not one freight rate discrepancy or anomaly has been removed. In fact the disparity has been widened as a result of inflation and other increases. The discrepancy between long and short haul rates still exists, as does the discrepancy in freight rates between raw and processed products. There is also the issue of rapeseed as it applies in the discriminatory application of freight rates in western Canada. My colleagues will deal with that in more detail.
The discrepancy in freight rate groupings still exists. These discrepancies continue to exist, notwithstanding the fact that in 1975 there was an agreement with the then ministers of transport of the western provinces and the then minister of transport, Mr. Marchand. These matters had been agreed upon and initiatives were to be taken. There was a short communique issued in February, 1975, in which it was said in respect of Mr. Marchand:
-he will propose a legislative amendment to reduce the rate differential anomalies between raw and finished products and in the interim will consult with the provinces and take measures necessary to correct urgent anomalies. Specifically the minister said he will recommend to his colleagues immediate steps within the existing legal structure to reduce the long-standing rapeseed products differential anomaly.
What do we hear today from the Minister of Transport? On October 20, as reported at page 59 of Hansard, the minister said:
On the question of equity, this is a matter of serious concern to us, as we have expressed over the years our belief in the need for greater equity in freight rates between processed and unprocessed products. There are very significant financial implications. We have been discussing this with the provinces in an attempt to reach some rational conclusion about what processing should take place, because the natural advantage in the prairie region does take place there.
That is just more words and more procrastination. Nothing has been done, nothing but more equivocating.
I turn to the question of grain handling where we have a glorious commitment. The commitment in 1974 was that the total grain handling system, from the grainery to the ships in
April 25, 1978

the harbour, would be revamped, and new systems introduced. What do we have? We have continued congestion in the port of Vancouver. We are now 35 million bushels behind our shipping target for the year. We have continued delays in loading. On any given day, there are an average of 24 ships waiting in the harbour. Elevators on the prairies are congested. Demurrage costs continue to pile up, some as high as $5,000 per ship per day.
Who pays that?

I will tell you who pays that. The farmer pays it, further reducing his income level which has declined by some 54 per cent since 1975, translated in terms of 1975 dollars. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture calls it a horrendous drop. More important, Canada continues to lose its reputation as a reliable supplier of grain in the export market. Its reputation is becoming tarnished and deteriorated. That is the sad fact of the matter.
We were to have had an expansion of the utilization of the port of Churchill. Those initiatives continue to be delayed. Prince Rupert has once again surfaced. It seems to surface during every pre-election campaign. There has been another commitment. However, if we are really honest about it, we will not see any improvement in the utilization of that port for five or six years.
Since 1973 we have heard about the necessity of a rail link to bypass the Fraser Canyon, the Clinton-Ashcroft link. Although it was promised in 1973, nothing has been done.
What about the grain handling system, the great revamping, and the great new system that was supposed to be introduced? It still takes an average of 23 days for a car to be loaded with grain, leave the country elevator point, go to Vancouver, and return. Those are not my statistics but statistics of the Hall report and Snavely report. It takes 23 days for a trainload of grain to get from the country elevator to the harbour and back for another load. I think it is fair to say that even hon. members could probably walk faster than that. We have seen no progress, no improvement in that area whatsoever. What is sad is that this situation continues to prevail in spite of the fact that we have seen a great deal of branch line abandonment on the prairies, a great deal of rationalization of the grain handling system, a great deal of consolidation of the elevator system, all of which have cost the prairie producer more money because he is obliged to deliver his grain further.
Speaking of branch line abandonment and elevator consolidation, it is interesting to recall what the present Minister of Transport had to say during the election campaign of 1974. A report in The Globe and Mail of June 10 of that year reads as follows:
Countering opposition that he is out to close small grain elevators situated close to farms, Mr. Lang declared that the small elevators would remain as long as farmers wanted them.
He went on to say at Lloydminster, as reported in the June 11, 1974, edition of the Winnipeg Free Press:
Transportation
As long as the Liberal party forms the government and as long as producers wish to continue to deliver to the elevators of their choice not one rail line will be abandoned.
More hollow, shallow, empty promises, Mr. Speaker.
I believe producers are prepared to play their part in improving the grain handling system, but the government, the railways, and the elevator companies all have to do their share. Leadership lies with the federal government. My party recognizes that it is a government responsibility. But the fact remains that the party sitting across the way has failed to deliver. The promises to which I have referred by no means represent the totality of the government's transportation package which was unveiled in 1974. Those vote-catching promises, without any real meaning, uttered without any sincerity, are probably consistent with the Liberal approach.
The party opposite thrives and survives by misleading the people. It is likely that nothing new will emerge from the upcoming campaign. Perhaps there will be a repetition, a rehashing of the old promises. However, I am sure the people will not be fooled for ever because, after all, most of those promises have been floating around ever since the Western Economic Conference of 1973. We all remember that in 1974 leadership was said to be the issue in the election. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the honesty of that leadership will be very much an issue in the minds of most Canadians.
In 1974 Liberal propagandists were saying:
The issue-the overwhelming issue-is leadership. The answer for anyone who is willing to take a good look at the record is obvious. Prime Minister Trudeau and his team of Liberal candidates are asking for your support July 8th.
But we have to ask this question: who is likely to do the best job of fulfilling the commitments which were made during the election campaign? That is what we have to ask ourselves.
Hear, hear!

Consider the record when it comes to fulfilling the commitments which were made. What has become of those sweeping plans, those radical departures from past methods, those comprehensive programs we heard so much about? What became of the idea of world leadership in transportation? We can probably summarize all this in one phrase: all we have received following those lofty promises amounts to nothing more than the Otto Lang user-pay concept. What has been done in this field? I will give the House a few examples.
The government tried to eliminate or dismantle the "at and east" rates which are a very important tool of economic development for the Atlantic provinces. The minister tried to do this on three occasions. He doubled the Seaway tolls. He proposed a 533 per cent increase in user fees at airports.
For most people.

For most people, as my hon. friend reminds me. He increased the tolls on the ferries by as much as 70 per cent in some cases-I have in mind the province of British Columbia. The gap in freight rates brought about by discriminatory rates and the anomalies to which I referred

April 25, 1978
Transportation
earlier, is ever widening, and the glib promises made during the campaign of 1974 are by now nothing more than a distant ideal-unless, of course, one happens to be the present Minister of Transport-he has a different version of user-pay for himself.
On behalf of my party I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that we reject Otto Lang's concept of the user-pay philosophy.
Hear, hear!

It has become a symbol of economic and political tension between the federal government and the provinces, between users and carriers, and I submit it is incompatible with the political, social, economic, and geographical dimensions of Canada. Furthermore, it leads to discrimination and decreases opportunities for economic growth and positive regional economic development.
I turn, now, to the Hall report. I say to you, sir, that my party endorses the Hall recommendations not only as a transportation charter for the west but also as an economic manifesto. This being the case, we are deeply disturbed by the minister's foot dragging in implementing the major recommendations of the report. There are some 92 recommendations in all. Six have been implemented, four have been partially implemented, 24 are the subject of further study, and 58 have not yet been acted upon. The Hall report must be viewed as a total package, a total concept for the economic development of western Canada.
The minister acted with great haste in the area of branch line abandonment, but it is interesting to note that he proceeded at a snail's pace when it came to removing the anomalies as between freight rates on raw and processed products. He has failed to make an unequivocal statement with respect to the Crowsnest Pass freight rates and the way in which the government would handle the gap between the Crow rate and that which would be viewed as a fair rate for the movement of grain.
As I understand it, the Minister of Transport has not even invited Mr. Justice Emmett Hall to discuss the implications of his report. That is very disturbing. There are a number of major recommendations in the Hall report which must be implemented, and we as a party would implement them very quickly and work together with Mr. Justice Hall in implementing them. Far too many specific recommendations which would revitalize processing activity in western Canada, broaden and strengthen its economic infrastructure, are in that document to let it sit around and gather dust on the shelf. We feel very strongly about that.
In conclusion, I want to outline some directions and some initiatives which we, as a party, feel are important in terms of developing and implementing a national transportation policy. We believe that transportation is a vital instrument of national unity. We believe it to be key to balanced economic growth, and we believe that it must be a positive tool of regional economic development.

We believe that a new transportation act is needed to serve Canada throughout the eighties and on into the twenty-first century and to reflect the fact that transportation must be a positive tool for regional economic development. Transportation must respond to national, regional, and urban challenges and realities. It must recognize the necessity of further processing and manufacturing of our resources, particularly our renewable resources, in those areas where they are grown, produced or located. We believe that it is the responsibility and the duty of the federal government to define national transportation goals, objectives, and priorities. The federal government must provide leadership in this area. These goals, objectives, and priorities must be developed, however, through meaningful and continuing consultation with the provinces. There must be a permanent mechanism for this to take place because transportation is very important to every region of Canada economically, socially, and politically.
We believe that consideration should be given to the establishment of a council of transport ministers composed of the federal minister and his ten provincial counterparts plus representatives from the Yukon and Northwest Territories. We believe that this would serve not only as a mechanism for development of priorities in national transportation but-
Order, please. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired. He may continue with unanimous consent. Does the hon. member have unanimous consent to continue?
Agreed.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and I thank hon. members for allowing me additional time. I assure the House that I shall not abuse this privilege. I simply want to confine my remarks to some initiatives and directions which we would like to place before the House at this time in connection with the motion we are debating.
We believe that such a mechanism would be very useful and helpful in developing priorities, goals, and objectives for national transportation but, more important, it would promote understanding and, I believe, would result in national support for any priorities and initiatives which may be taken and which have to be taken in the national interest.
Having defined the goals and objectives, the regulatory body, the Canadian Transport Commission, should have its role very clearly defined. It should be responsible for the implementation and execution of the national policy which is defined, and it should function with a minimum of political interference. We feel that this is needed to provide the degree of stability and certainty which is urgently required at this point in time in the transportation industry, because there has been too much political interference, political manipulation, and ad hoc measures. It is necessary to restore confidence in the transportation industry if we are to improve our productivity, the reliability of our transportation systems, and our technology. It is important to have that climate of stability and confidence in order to attract the kind of capital investment
April 25, 1978

which will be required to develop and expand the systems we need in this country for the twenty-first century.
We hold in very high regard the importance of the regions of this country, and having regard to the regional needs and the uniqueness of the regions of this country we feel that consideration should be given to the establishment of a western and an Atlantic arm of the Canadian Transport Commission. This would provide an opportunity to respond quickly in meeting the regional needs and demands of users of the various modes. Furthermore, it would serve to speed up the regulatory process, which needs a lot of speeding up. It has become entwined in red tape and over-dominated by bureaucratic devices. That operation clearly has to be streamlined.
The act has to be clearly defined, and there have to be new mechanisms put in place for seeking and obtaining adequate redress for the problems which crop up from time to time. Such a mechanism would ensure that adequate and effective service is provided at a minimum cost, and would monitor and correct such things as freight rates, equipment supply, maintenance and modernization of plant and equipment facilities. We believe that this could be achieved without adding to the size of the existing Canadian Transport Commission. That would basically mean a regionalization of the operation to take into account the regional realities and the diversity of this country.
We feel that consideration should also be given to the establishment of a national advisory council on transportation, and that the users of all modes of transportation should be invited to participate. We feel that this is necessary so that the goals and objectives which are defined in a national transportation policy could be geared to the needs of users. We think that is very important, and it is something which has not been happening.
There has not been enough consultation in the development and administration of transportation policy. I see that the minister is smiling. His version of consultation is perhaps somewhat different from the version of hon. members on this side of the House. To hon. members opposite it is consult and "We will do what we want to do anyway". That is really not the way we describe consultation. We feel that the role of the Ministry of Transport should be reviewed and assessed with a view to reducing the monopolistic role which it now plays. That role often finds itself in a conflict of interest position. It was described adequately and appropriately by the Air Transport Association of Canada, which said that users view themselves as captive tenants of a monopolistic landlord. Airports are built and facilities are established by the MOT without any consultation, and without any advice from the people who use those facilities.

speechtext: You are out of date.

If I am outdated, there should be no problem in accepting the amendment to Bill C-4 which would enshrine the kind of consultative process which we think is necessary, and which, incidentally, is supported by all the users
Transportation
involved with the Department of Transport. You have accepted one, sir, and there is another one on the order paper. If the minister is saying they will accept the amendment which is now on the order paper in my name, I can assure him the bill will have speedy passage. The fact is, there is no appeal. Consultation is non-existent.
We think that MOT would do well to work toward divesting itself of its responsibilities in areas which might be better served by the private sector or by other levels of government. When you look at the conflict which arose with regard to the Edmonton International Airport, the desire to have new and better facilities there to accommodate the tremendous number of people who will be visiting that city during the Commonwealth Games, you find that the provincial government wants to help the federal government, but there is no co-operation from the federal government. There has been consultation, but there is no co-operation.
Perhaps other levels of government could involve themselves in supplying this kind of infrastructure, not deviating from the power and authority of MOT to lay down standards and of CTC to ensure that those standards are maintained, but there may well be another area in which we can expedite the development of our transportation infrastructure. We believe that immediate steps should be taken to stimulate innovation and to improve productivity in the transportation sector. The appropriate fiscal policy and incentives are necessary there.
We believe that steps must be taken to increase private investment in our transportation systems. We know that over the next number of years a huge infusion of capital will be required to provide the infrastructure and the equipment necessary to expand and to strengthen the basic transportation network to meet future demands.
Most important of all, what we need to get on with the job of building an efficient and effective transportation system is a climate of openness, a climate of trust, and a climate of co-operation. We have the most secretive government in the history of this country, and that is part and parcel of the problem. It is not only secretive, it refuses to consult, and it fails to co-operate. We believe that if we are to get Canada working again, if we are to get the most of our transportation system, we must do it together and, in order to achieve that, we must work together.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion moved by my good friend, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). One could think of another ten items at least to add to this motion, but it covers most of the ground.
The preamble to the motion states that the minister has sidetracked promises made by his own party and by his government in 1974. That is true and obviously plain to people all over Canada. They made promises that were glowing and that warmed the hearts of the public when they promised to abandon the outmoded freight rate structure and to remove regional freight inequities. They promised that rates at less than cost of service would apply in special cases, but instead

April 25, 1978
Transportation
they are trying to give us the user pay concept. They even tried to enshrine that concept in Bill C-33 in the last session, which, I gather, now is withdrawn as a result of opposition even from government backbenchers. Not only did they renege on those promises, but now they want to do away with the Crowsnest statutory grain rates, about the only benefit left to western Canada. They want to do away with the "at and east" rates on grain and flour shipments through the maritime ports, creating unemployment there, as if there were not already enough.
The federal government, with the capitulation of the Liberal and Conservative provincial governments in the Atlantic provinces, plans to tamper with the Maritime Freight Rates Act assistance. The government promised that not one railway branch line would be abandoned so long as the producers wanted to use it and the elevators continued to operate. What has happened to that promise?
About a month ago, for example, the Prairie Rail Action Committee-a little committee that was set up so that both the minister and the railroads can get their way, sometimes in spite of what the railroads want-recommended the abandonment of two lines, and everyone, including their railroads, the elevator companies, the producers, and the communities concerned, wanted to keep them. The Liberals promised a transportation information act to provide Ottawa with access to all information it needs to formulate freight rate policies, including companies' costs. We still have to rely on the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to find out how much the president of CPR is paid.
They promised a national freight car leasing corporation. We did not get it. Every day there are reports of some Canadian commodity unable to reach market because there is a shortage of railway equipment.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised to abandon the outmoded freight rate structure, one based on the competitive market place. What has happened is a greater reliance on market place competition and profitability, not a lessening of reliance.
The Prime Minister promised that a Liberal government would provide $290 million in urban transit assistance to provinces and municipalities. That promise has not been kept. The actual program announced last fall involves little or no new funding. They juggled the books. It will take $100 million from the commuter services program announced in 1975 but never implemented, and $130 million from the railway relocation and grade crossing fund. That is a program that needs more funds, not funds being taken away from it, but that is how they try to fool people into thinking that that promise of the Prime Minister was kept.
The Prime Minister promised to establish transcontinental excursion trains to supplement existing transcontinental services. That means more trains, not less. Instead, they plan to phase out one of the Montreal to Toronto to Vancouver services, or substantially reduce it.
The Prime Minister promised to bring into service high speed passenger trains to the central corridor. That was four

years ago. The minister finally got around to getting some LRC trains ordered just in the past year. These high speed trains are a laugh. The train from Ottawa to Toronto still takes five and three quarter hours. It travels at an average speed of 48 miles an hour. Another train takes six hours and five minutes and travels at an average speed of 46 miles an hour. If that is the vision of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) of high speed intercity trains, we do not need that kind of vision. That will not entice people to get out of their cars or get off short haul plane flights and get on to trains. It will militate even further against them wanting to do so.
VIA Rail, which I think had great plans and great ideas, has been stepped on by the ministry. It wanted to do a good job, but will not be allowed to do it. They will not be provided with the funding that is required to implement the Prime Minister's own promise. They do not intend to provide train service between Edmonton and Calgary. Although the Minister of Transport has announced that some LRC trains are going to operate in the west and in the maritimes, VIA Rail has not provided a commitment that these units will supplement existing passenger train service. We suspect that instead it will replace existing passenger train service in which there is also some reduction.
The motion of the hon. member indicates that the Minister of Transport has failed consistently to manage Canadian transportation policy in an efficient and effective manner. That is true, but also it is true of the old line party administrations which governed previous to this one. As long as pofitabil-ity and competition are the cornerstones of transportation policy, we will remain in the same mess with inefficient duplicate systems, energy wasteful systems, further lay-offs in our transportation industry, depressed regional economies, and regional disparities.
I find it passing strange that the official opposition would call upon the government to abandon its user pay policy, when those same hon. members advocate profitability and competition. In order to attain profitability and competition, it is necessary to maintain user pay. One cannot have it both ways. I wish hon. members of the official opposition would stop attempting to work both sides of the street.
The official opposition persuaded the government to amend the legislation to require Air Canada to operate in contemplation of profit. That can mean only one thing: reduced service to Atlantic Canada, the prairies, and outlying regions which do not have the volume of traffic to sustain a commercial enterprise or, in other words, where it is not profitable. My Conservative friends cannot have it both ways on that one either.
The Conservative governments of Newfoundland and New Brunswick not only agreed to allow the federal government to do away with passenger services, but agreed to let the maritime freight assistance act fall by the wayside. Canada does not need Tories. The Alberta Conservative government was
April 25, 1978

not only opposed to letting rapeseed products qualify for the statutory grain rates, but suggested that domestic shipments of grain be taken off the Crow rate to Thunder Bay. The hon. member for Vegreville and his colleagues from Alberta should attempt to have that straightened out by the Conservative government in that province.
Activities are ongoing in the prairie provinces which cause me to want to move an amendment to the hon. member's motion. I am confident my amendment will receive approval from most members of the House. It is a worth-while addition, and I hope hon. members will agree with it. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes):
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a semi-colon, and by adding thereafter an additional paragraph:
(e) to reject the Prairie Rail Action Committee recommendations to close down the Liberty to Dilke and Eston to Lacadena rail lines, and to bring forward legislation to set up the Prairie Rail Authority.
The Hall commission made recommendations concerning these two particular instances, as well as a number of others. In the case of the Colonsay subdivision, which is a heavy grain line, the recommendation was that it should be maintained. The Prairie Rail Action Committee, which is a creature of the Minister of Transport, recommends that a significant portion of it should be abandoned. This would accomplish perhaps the aims of the minister, but both railroads feel that it should be maintained, not to mention the producers and the Hall Commission.
The affected communities have been betrayed, as well as the intention of the Hall commission recommendation. When I questioned members of the commission about this particular line I asked them, if this line was so important and should be maintained, why could it not be put into the basic network, instead of having it come under the Prairie Rail Authority. Their response to me was reasonable. They wanted it to come under the Prairie Rail Authority so that it would receive fast rehabilitation and upgrading, and then be transferred to the basic network. That is why the Hall commission recommended that, so that it would receive priority treatment in upgrading and then be returned to the basic network. Instead of that, the minister's committee recommended that a significant portion of it be abandoned, which betrayed those communities as well as the recommendations of the Hall commission.
The Prairie Rail Authority should be an essential tool for the rehabilitation of hundreds of rail lines in the three prairie provinces. Instead of that, the minister has a Prairie Rail Action Committee, which is designed to implement what the railroads and the minister wanted in the first place. After all the hearings, the consultations, and the fine work done by the Hall commission, it is being subverted in this backdoor manner which the minister and his committee chose. The same thing applies to the other subdivisions which were mentioned in my amendment. The people out west are worried that there is more to come. They are worried on good grounds.
The first vice-president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, on April 19, 1978, said the following:
Transportation
The pool may be forced into a greater degree of rationalization and consolidation than it would like in its country elevator system.
Mr. Donald M. Lockwood, the first vice-president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, made that comment. That organization is the largest farmer-owned grain handling organization in the world. Also he pointed out that the pool projected the reduction of its country elevator system to a network of 600 operating units at 500 locations. Also Mr. Lockwood indicated that PRAC may go further than the pool had projected in rail line abandonment. Their plans for the construction of new, upgraded, and high throughput country elevators have been thrown askew. Now their planning has to wait. Their intentions to build and rebuild country elevators for their members and the grain producers at dozens of shipping points, are in jeopardy. This is because of the recommendations the Prairie Rail Action Committee has come up with already, as well as other ones which we are afraid it will make.
The Minister of Transport should reject those recommendations. Also he should assure us in a concrete manner that the recommendations of the Hall commission, in the main, will be implemented and that he is committed to them. If not, the Minister of Transport, his colleagues, and Liberal candidates will rue that day. Of course that day will be called election day.
If the minister does not provide an irrevocable commitment to maintain the statutory grain rates, we have news for him. I am not only referring to the maintenance of those rates, but also to an extension of them to apply to grain products. It is not a subsidy to western grain producers or the processors of our grain products. It is a benefit to the nation as a whole. It allows us to compete in the markets of central Canada and around the world. Because of our geography and climate, the nation as a whole should share in the cost of moving raw products as well as processed ones. There should be an extension of the statutory grain rate principle to other processors and producers of raw products in the prairie provinces, as well as in the Atlantic provinces and the other outlying regions of Canada. That is only fair, if these regions are to have further economic development. If these regions are to have a fair crack at the markets of central Canada, the United States and other countries around the world, we must not handicap them with a freight rate system which causes their costs to rise to a point where they are unable to compete.
What has the government done instead of that? It helped finance an oil seed processing plant in Windsor, Ontario. They do not even grow it there. What does that do to rapeseed processing in western Canada? I understand that that plant will be capable of processing soybeans, peanuts, sunflower seeds, and palm oil. This will mean that the western Canadian rapeseed producers will be played off against the American soybean producers. It threatens the rapeseed processing industry and the other oil seed processing industries in western Canada.

April 25, 1978
Transportation
It is bad enough if the competition comes from other countries, but when it comes from within our own boundaries and harms people in a major portion of our country, it cannot be justified by anybody who would wish to do something about reducing alienation and increasing national unity. There is no reason why we cannot do this. The same should apply to our transportation industry when it comes to moving people as well as goods.
It has long been maintained that transportation companies should be publicly owned and operated. There are many instances in the transportation industry in which competition is taking place and it is not working. Such a position was even maintained by a former minister of transport. If you are going to maintain competition and profitability as a cornerstone, there must be discrimination against people and goods because of where they happen to live or where the goods happen to be produced. Unless we set up a transportation system that both cross subsidizes and directly subsidizes and equalizes transportation costs around this country, then that discrimination that we have been getting all these years is going to continue because the transportation companies will, quite rightly, say "It is not profitable and we are not going to do it." Because of this, another part of the country loses service entirely or has it reduced, and rates and fares go up to a level where the people who must use them cannot afford to do so.
What we need is a rail passenger service of a frequency and quality that will attract people out of automobiles and from short and medium haul plane runs. Those passenger services must be integrated, not only among the railroads but with other modes of travel such as bus and air. This scheme would allow people to buy a package of transportation with fast schedules at a reasonable cost.
I could not believe my eyes when I saw the proposal put forth by VIA Rail. To take one rail trip from Montreal to Regina one of the alternatives was to sit in the railway station in Winnipeg for nearly nine hours to make a connection to another train. That is really no way to improve railway passenger systems, and it will not entice people to get out of their cars and on to the train.
VIA Rail is being started off with a count against it. I believe the minister has already advised VIA Rail that they-
Order. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted speaking time has expired. He may continue if he has the unanimous consent of the House. Does he have unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, as my colleague from Vegre-ville has done, I too will not abuse the kindness of the House in the few extra minutes that I have been granted.
As I was saying, the minister, his department, and the government have told VIA Rail that they will be unable to operate a rail passenger system across this country to the

extent that they proposed. When the transportation committee heard the president of VIA Rail a number of months ago, he made a presentation to us that had us all delighted. We all complimented him and, indeed, we embellished upon it and promised him the support of the committee. Since then, however, there has been a steady erosion and reduction in the plans that VIA Rail has in mind. I would not blame the president, Mr. Roberts, if he resigned in protest tomorrow. In fact I would be willing to applaud him because it may be the kind of hit on the head that the government needs.
If VIA Rail is going to provide the attractive, efficient, safe, comfortable, and fast alternative in travel to the public it was meant to, it is going to require not only re-equipping but extra trains. There is no reason why we cannot be implementing, over the next two or three years, 125-mile an hour passenger trains on runs over 400, 500 and 600 miles in western Canada. It should already be in place between Quebec City and Windsor and it is not. There have been improvements in the Turbo, but it can be improved more and should be, if it is to operate at higher speeds. In a couple of years we should be looking at speeds of 150 miles an hour on the trackage we now have, provided there is some improvement in our signal systems and some curves straightened out on the roadbed. Generally, the trackage is capable now of taking trains at those speeds.
If we are going to reduce automobile travel and put an end to the nonsense of short-haul, commercial aircraft runs, in which money is wasted in the form of energy costs incurred in the use of airports which are in excess of what the public costs would be for high-speed, intercity rail passenger service, and down the road one or two years from now, if we are unfortunate enough to have a Liberal government, it may say, "Well, we tried VIA Rail and passenger business did not go up, so we are going to cancel some more". It is a self-fulfilling wish. If there is no incentive and no attraction for people to ride on the passenger train, then it can be reduced some more. That is the way the minister is setting it up. That is the way this government wants it, which is a tragedy as it does not serve the national interest as well as we think it should.
There are many other ways, Mr. Speaker, of making our transportation system in the area of moving people more efficient. There should be effort directed toward improving the use of ticketing, reservations, and downtown passenger terminals, which all modes of transportation use. The minister is perfectly aware of what we are trying to have implemented in Regina, and I hope we succeed. We hope to have in one terminal the bus service, rail service, the airport ticket office, airport limousines and transit stops all of which would orginate and terminate there. There would be ample taxi stands and private parking.
It is nonsense to have the Air Canada ticket office in the very prestigious Toronto-Dominion Bank building in Regina where there are only two parking places, and they are two-minute zones. The facility is cramped, and neither the public nor the employees like it, but there it sits. Yet, we have the railway station, most of which is unused, centrally located, with lots of parking. This is where Air Canada should be told
April 25, 1978

to put their downtown ticket office, but instead they want to continue with that elitist attitude of having it in an expensive new bank building, which does not properly serve the people of that city. This is also the case in many other areas of Canada, and I only use Regina as an example. This is another area of deficiency, and I am certain that the bus companies and airlines would be willing to co-operate because it would reduce their costs and eliminate a lot of duplication.
The electrification of railway lines is another area into which we should be moving. I hope to get the figures soon, but I would guess that if you were to electrify the railway lines, the main and secondary lines between Thunder Bay and Rocky Mountain, the amount of diesel fuel saved would be equal to what our farmers in the west use to put in their crops. This would be a sensible innovation, and we have the capacity to produce the electricity for it. The cost of electrification would be approximately $100,000 per mile according to figures I can get from engineers. That is where the profit is-it profits the whole nation and improves our use of energy through a more efficient way to move trains, yet we are not doing anything about it.
We believe this kind of program for a 25,000 volt overhead electrification system on the main lines should be launched immediately, particularly on the prairies and through the mountains to the Pacific coast. That kind of imagination is required for the rebuilding and enlarging of our transportation systems. The present piecemeal, haphazard way of doing it- the continuous effort to make profitability and competition the priorities in transportation-these things are self defeating. They got us into the mess in the first place, yet the government and the Conservative party cling to the nineteenth century concepts in transportation that most other countries, socialist and capitalist, discarded a long time ago. This is the kind of fundamental change required in transportation in this country, but we are not getting it.
Many people thought the election promises made in 1974 by the Prime Minister would move us in that direction, but most of those promises have not been kept and, indeed, in some cases the opposite was done. It was a betrayal, and if the minister thinks the public will trust similar promises in the coming campaign he is just fooling himself. He will not fool Canadians.
Unless and until we have a government with the political will to make this fundamental change in transportation policy, and a more efficient organization, we will make no headway. We need buses that stop at every little town and take people 50 or 100 miles, trains that do not stop so often but travel at 125 miles an hour on 500 mile trips-if that is downtown to downtown it is almost equivalent to flying time. The train from downtown Ottawa to downtown Montreal takes less time than the flight, yet we have this nonsense of three or four engine jets wasting thousands of gallons of fuel on a flight of 120 miles. That is just stupid. The government seems to have no will to do anything about it, however, and I suspect a Con-
Adjournment Motion
servative government would leave everything to competition and profitability.
This party would make a change. I believe we can provide transportation for people and goods while making the most efficient use of all modes, gaining the confidence of the workers on all modes, and providing a service on a shared pay basis. People will be willing to share the cost with their fellow Canadians-to share the cost of things like statutory rates for grain and grain products and for other primary and natural products from the prairies, the far north, or the Atlantic region. We all share those costs; that is called confederation. It puts an end to alienation and strengthens national unity.
The transportation policies of past years have contributed to the alienation not only of Quebec but of other regions of Canada. Surely this fundamental change must occur in transportation, because it is an essential part of a renewed and lasting confederation. It is an essential tool.
The gentlemen in power in the 1870's and the 1880's had more foresight than governments of recent years. They regarded transportation as a tool of national policy. At least they looked at it in that way in principle. If the Minister of Transport implements that kind of policy, he will have made, and will be applauded for, a real contribution to national unity and a stronger confederation.
Order, please. The House has heard the terms of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin).

The House resumed consideration of the motion of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski):
That in the opinion of this House, the Minister of Transport has consistently failed to manage Canadian transportation policy in an efficient and effective manner and implement the promises of the 1974 election campaign, and the House calls upon the government to take positive action:

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is apparent from the speeches of the lead spokesmen for the Conservative party and the New Democratic Party how much progress has been made in the field of transportation in the last several years.
The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) mentioned that my predecessor said we would be coming forward with a comprehensive statement in regard to transport, and he asked about that. I presume he has forgotten what has been a charter document, issued in June, 1975, and the basis in philosophy and analysis of many of the solutions we have since been applying to problems of transportation. In a few short years, what my predecessor described as a mess in transportation has been put right.
Further evidence is contained in the speeches of hon. members who preceded me. In saying what they would do about transportation they supported in almost every case the positive things we have done. When the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) calls for an integrated, intermodal transfer system, with common usage terminals, he is quoting one of our policy documents. When he says he wants the Crow rate retained he knows that I have made it very clear that any change in regard to that would have to reflect western interests and western analyses of the problems that may be created between grain and beef, and nothing else.
He says he wants to look at electrification. I presume he has forgotten that, just as the Hall commission was completing its report and recommending studies on electrification, we were
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
already producing studies on electrification and that experimental work on it is in progress at the present time.
The hon. member for Vegreville has put his party's views in regard to the field of transportation. I presume he is unveiling his platform. He wants a permanent method of consultation with provincial governments. He has forgotten that we have set up with each region of the country a permanent form of consultation and it is exactly what those regions want, because it recognizes in most cases the problems to be faced are regionally analysed in a superior way. In addition, ministers of transport can meet whenever they want to. He says he wants the Canadian Transport Commission's role defined. The bill he talked out in the last session-he joined in filibustering-
I never even spoke on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
He also said that he wanted a western branch of the Canadian Transport Commission, enunciating what apparently is a platform policy he has taken from an announcement I made several months ago. That was our view as to what should be done in relation to the Hall commission recommendation that a prairie rail authority had exactly that kind of function and that kind of authority. We announced that was our intention and we hope to proceed in that way in the near future.
The hon. member for Vegreville wants consultation. Any organization significantly involved in transportation with federal jurisdiction involvement would agree that full consultation about changes we want to make or propose to make has been the order of the day these past several years. In many cases, as in the case of landing fees affecting light aircraft, we responded, and changed the form of the charge being made to meet the wishes of the people, who were, in that way, consulted. That puts the lie to the hon. member's suggestion that our view of consultation is to do what we intended to do originally.
The hon. member for Vegreville did refer to certain proposals that we had which we have not been able to carry out in full. He referred particularly to the urban transportation assistance policy where, instead of the exact program we had intended in the 1974 campaign, we produced an urban transportation assistance program worth $230 million over a five-year period. This includes a significant amount of $100 million of new money.
I recommend to the hon. member that he look at the nature of the program as it portrays our approach to transportation problems with the provinces and municipalities in this area where theirs is the prime responsibility. Under the urban transportation assistance policy we have set up, there is a great deal of flexibility for the provincial interest involved, speaking on behalf of its various municipalities to see its view expressed in terms of direct concrete results. In other words the federal government, in this case, has made available a specific amount of money for each province. It is basically saying that the provincial priorities in the broad field of urban transportation assistance are the ones that will determine how that money is
April 25, 1978

used. This is an important step in eliminating red tape and the complexity in our assistance to municipalities and provinces.
We have produced, and it is on the order paper, a ports act to revise and completely put into a new framework the ports policy of this country. It is a ports policy which has been generally welcomed across the country, particularly by those who are most involved in ports. It is designed in keeping with our policy and our principles to give as much local autonomy as possible to vital port commissions for each of our great and important ports throughout the country. That would be our intention as soon as we can find the legislative time to go forward with that important piece of legislation. It is there, and it solves an important problem in regard to organization of our ports.
The fact of the legislation being there and not having been dealt with has not stopped us from moving ahead rapidly with major port improvements in Canada. Announcements, sod turnings, and opening of port facilities in Halifax, Saint John, Montreal, Quebec City, Vancouver and Prince Rupert, to name the principal east and west coast ports of Canada, have shown that these improvements have been carried out. These improvements, which total many millions of dollars, are extremely important.
We have moved forward on the issue of freight rates. This is something which a Conservative government only tackled by setting up a Royal commission. This Royal commission recommended certain formulae and an approach to rates that was basically free and competitive rather than controlled. This has not worked. We now intend to put this right by introducing controls on long and short-haul rates so that the short-haul rate cannot exceed the long-haul rate. We intend to put maximum rates in place. These are not just to apply to those who are technically captive shippers but to those who are charged too much in any case and in every case.
When this measure in the form of Bill C-33 was before this House it was clear that the Conservative opposition at least intended to take a long time over it, and we were not able to invest adequate time to see its passage. They made that stand clear to us in private conversation as well as their conduct in the House. I think it is particularly sad that western members were once again stopping an important matter of interest-
What is his name?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
-and vital interest to the west, just as they did in the case of stabilization-forcing us to take many more years to accomplish what we need to accomplish for the west.
That will come better after the next election if, as I expect, we will have more western members on this side of the House.
No; we will be over there.
We will be there and you will be here.

Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the opposition likes to excite concern about the practical, sensible, financial approach to transportation-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: User-pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
-that in many cases we try to apply. The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) says user-pay.
It is a phrase they like to use to mislead people.
We do not think it is right that those who ride on a bus should pay their whole way while those who fly or go by rail or go by automobile get subsidy support for their way of moving. In areas where we can support these various forms of passenger travel it is better if we leave the system even in terms of the way taxpayers' dollars are used, so that the person choosing a transportation system chooses it according to his own view of how he weighs the value of the privacy of his automobile, the economy of the bus, the additional comfort of the train, or the speed at the great cost of air travel.
What we should not do is abuse the taxpayer by using taxpayers' dollars in one way or another to induce a person to travel in a way he would not travel if he were making the choice on his own. That is what a sensible financing policy in regard to transportation means.
What it has meant in regard to our airport policy is that increasingly we do consult the airlines, and the spokesmen who have to market the service, about what is needed in regard to airport services. We find that when they know they will be accountable for the amounts that are spent, they suddenly become more practical minded in regard to the demands they make concerning facilities which should be put in place.
As long as it was simply the taxpayer paying for an airport facility there was not the same regard as there is now under the new policy. This will be demonstrated step by step, not by airports which were built while the old policy was in place, but those which are being built now. It will explain why we are not moving forward with major changes and rebuilding at the Ottawa airport. We have no present intention to do that on the basis of current indications. Instead we have found a modest way of making improvements which are desirable and sensible but at really very low cost. That is the kind of change which happens when one applies a principle of sense and responsibility to the financing of airport construction-
What about Mirabel?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext: An hon. member has referred to Mirabel. Mirabel was built before the introduction of this policy. Even at that it is an airport which will prove to be extremely useful, as will the Calgary airport.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
We have seen in the last couple of years in regard to two of our great transportation Crown corporations a complete turn-around of a past practice of inefficiency. Instead there has been a move toward effective provision of service. Both Canadian National and Air Canada have report-
