April 25, 1978
Transportation
ed profits in 1977. Payments of dividends on investments made by Canadians will begin. This is a reversal of the trend as was so often the case in the past when efficiency and good service were unimportant.
We do not intend to look over the shoulder of good management in those corporations, under pressure from spokesmen in this House on the opposition side who will want this or that done in terms of management, as though we should be running those corporations on a day to day basis. We continue to resist that, and produce instead a document in which good and effective service can be provided by Canadian National and Air Canada more and more, in full and complete balance, competitive with other companies in the same or other modes of transportation.
Hon. members have seen what has happened in our policy with regard to rail passenger service. We have announced an intention to give rail passenger service in this country a fair and full trial. To do so, we have made it possible, through our direct purchase and a purchase by VIA Rail, to acquire ten new train sets of the light, rapid, comfortable kind, which will be made in Canada and put in service in Canada to attract more and more passengers to the rail mode throughout this country.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
The ten sets will allow us to have that improved service not only between the most populous cities in the country, but on the transcontinental service from ocean to ocean. Under the new management, which is putting together a new form of marketing and a unified ticketing system, we want a rededication to attract passengers back to the rail mode, not with heavy subsidies allowing rail to ride on the back of the bus system, but more and more in a way to attract passengers out of automobiles into public transportation. We believe this is possible and sensible in our revision of service.
Hon. members referred to the movement of freight by rail. The hon. member for Vegreville asked what we are doing in that regard. The railways are ordinarily expected to make the major move with regard to the provision of adequate capacity as movements are projected and foreseen. The railways have been doing a fairly competent job of that. To assist them to assure they would do the job, in each of the last two budgets there have been significant changes and improvements in the capital cost allowance for the railways so that their cash flow might be improved. They responded with plans to expand more rapidly their capacity where they foresaw that freight coming about.
The big exception of the railway's capability to do what is needed for freight has been in the area of grain. There, as the Snavely commission has identified, the railways receive very little for grain movement compared to the cost of moving it. The Hall commission stated there is a call upon the government to do additional things in the way of financing to ensure that the railways have the funds, notwithstanding the con-
[Mr. Lang.l
tinued existence of the longstanding statutory Crow rate on grain.
The government foresaw that before the Hall Commission recommendation. In our 1975 policy statement we made clear that where it is a matter of policy to maintain rates at a level below cost, the government should be willing to identify that policy and its cost, and pay the amount of money to the transportation system expected to bear the burden. Therefore, it would not have to pass the costs of that transportation system on to other people or, indeed, be inadequately provided for.
We responded to that spirit of need of an additional infusion of cash with the provision of 8,000 hopper cars for the movement of grain, at a cost of $255 million. Two western spokesmen speaking on transportation in the House today omitted to mention that very important investment, which was the first real important move toward improving our grain handling system in the way of capital and investment in some 40 years. I remind hon. members, with some dismay, that that includes a period of six years when the Diefenbaker government was in power. That western Prime Minister did not take any steps toward improving that grain handling and transportation system, except setting up one royal commission on transportation as a whole. We set up the Hall commission and the Snavely commission, and have been dedicating ourselves toward implementing their reports. In this moment of fiscal restraint we do not have the ability to move at once to pay to the railways what the Hall commission recommended, the whole of the difference between the Crow rate and what it costs to move grain. That recommendation was consistent with our 1975 policy statement.
What we did was immediate and of fundamental importance. The most important thing was to see that the railways went ahead with investment in those grain lines on the prairies which had been neglected. Within a matter of a few short weeks of the Hall commission report coming down, we transferred to the basic rail network the additional 1,813 miles which the Hall commission identified for that purpose, and we committed the first $100 million for the rail rehabilitation program in the prairie region. That is significant.
As a western member I am particularly pleased that, at a convention here in Ottawa in February, a resolution sponsored by the prairie provinces, under the leadership of Saskatchewan, was passed by that great Liberal convention of people assembled from all over the country.
Within a few short weeks that resolution, which recommended the allocation of $600 million for a further eight-year completion of the upgrading program, had been adopted as government policy. We were able to announce that in Regina at a cabinet meeting held there in March.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
After years and years of neglect, years and years of nothing having been done with regard to the grain handling system, we not only had the 8,000 hopper cars, but the commitment of the full amount of money required to put the
April 25, 1978

basic rail network, all of the branch lines which will be progressively transferred into it, into first class shape, at least for the carrying of the fully loaded aluminum hopper cars, if not in every case the steel ones. That is extremely important.
We also did the engineering almost immediately on the connections of one line to the other, as recommended by the Hall commission. We found those connections are in each case feasible. In several cases, we will be proceeding with them. One particular one in Vegreville is already completed.
The western CTC which the Hall commission recommended is something we will be proceeding with in the next session of parliament. We knew we could not in this session deal with the whole of the issue of the prairie rail authority to which the Hall commission referred. Therefore, we set up its equivalent in the Prairie Rail Action Committee. It is equivalent in so far as the important powers are concerned, which is to identify those pieces of track within the doubtful category where the Hall commission had not identified their future, and where the committee could recommend the permanence of those pieces of track which they think should be permanent.
We have had some of those recommendations. They have given us certainty where uncertainty, as was left by the commission report, would not have sufficed. That is why when setting up the Prairie Rail Action Committee and moving toward resolving these questions, we put our proposals and our action before 30 or more groups representing prairie farmers and prairie municipalities. We have had overwhelming endorsement of what we are doing. Certainty is what was wanted, certainty, and the rebuilding of lines identified as permanent. That is what we have been doing.
I remind hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, that we have in the Prairie Rail Action Committee recommendations a certain number of rail lines which that committee recommends be transferred to the permanent network. In several of those cases we have acted to move to transfer those lines and put them in our rebuilding programs. We have also moved to begin negotiations on the connections and the interchange of rail lines between CN and CP which was envisaged in the Hall commission report.
I want to remind the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, who moved the amendment, that when he speaks of Prairie Rail Action Committee recommendations in regard to the section from Liberty to Dilke, from Eston to Lacadena, these are recommendations only, and would first have to be considered by the Canadian Transport Commission before they could be acted upon, and if, as I propose, we set up a western arm of the Canadian Transport Commission they will be considered and acted upon there, no doubt with further hearings so that the communities concerned can be heard. What we have done on the positive side is something he chooses to ignore.
We have accepted the recommendation to go ahead with the permanence of the line from Watrous to Liberty, the permanence of the line from Wartime to Kyle, and included those
Transportation
lines in the basic network and in the program for rebuilding so that they will not just be lines of steel on a map or on the prairies without the substance to carry cars, but be in solide, first class shape. That, I think, is something the hon. member should recognize at this point in time, rather than leave great concern in the minds of people in the area about what is being done.
The Hall commission recommended action with respect to Churchill and Prince Rupert, and in both cases we have been taking that action. Last week I announced programs of $5 million and more for Churchill in connection with the installation of lighting, dredging, and improvement of facilities at the port and elevator, and the rehabilitation progam, to which I referred earlier, including $1.6 million for additional sidings at Herchmer on the way to Churchill. It is the very thing which is required in order to increase capacity for the carriage of grain to that port.
In the case of Prince Rupert, as hon. members know, we have announced a proposal to spend $28 million on that port to improve grain facilities and to provide additional facilities. A further $11 million or more is to be spent on the improvement of existing elevators so that more grain can be handled there and, of fundamental importance, an investment of $16.5 million is contemplated at Ridley Island in order to prepare the way for private investment by the grain trade, perhaps, I am happy to say, with the co-operation of others. I foresee this happening in a very large way.
We recognize the challenges. We recognize the challenge of continuing to increase our freight capacity through the mountains, for instance, and we have responded with the budget changes to which I have referred, thus allowing some additional double-tracking of rail so that increased capacity will be there. We are responding in that way because we foresee, with what I believe to be realistic optimism, not only the record of grain exports which we have already assured for this year but growth by about 200 million bushels over that amount in the several years to come. That is extremely important news for the prairies and, indeed, for all of Canada.
With the expansion at Prince Rupert we will have additional capacity because, in the opinion of those expert in selling our grain, the Canadian Wheat Board particularly, the bulk of the growth in our exports will be shipped through the west coast ports. We are therefore taking action. We are not simply standing by to see what may happen and see what is needed.
I could go on and on about other subjects. I could refer to air travel which, with our initiative, has moved forward with charter flights and charter competitive fares, initiatives which have led to airlines in this country not just Air Canada but all of them, becoming more efficient. It will result in their having a higher level of seat occupancy for the good of the passengers. I referred to Air Canada's profits, Mr. Speaker. It is significant that this profit reflected directly an improved efficiency of operation. The fare increases which occurred in the period can be shown to reflect only actual increases in the cost of base operations and that profit, instead of loss, has come from the fact that with the same kind of basic operation, and perhaps

even fewer flight operations, Air Canada has been carrying more passengers more passenger miles and is thereby becoming more effective and more efficient and is now able to offer lower fares, as well as showing a profit for the Canadian people.

The minister mentioned the railway rehabilitation program and referred specifically to the link at Vegreville. speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:

[Mr. Lang.l

Mr. Speaker, 1 am very happy that the motion moved by the Progressive Conservative Party concerns our Canadian transportation policy and blames the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) for having failed consistently, and I quote:
... to manage Canadian transportation policy in an efficient and effective manner and implement the promises of the 1974 election compaign, and the House calls upon the government to take positive action:
(a) to abandon the user pay concept and develop over-all transportation
objectives which will enhance national harmony, reduce regional disparities
and promote balanced economic growth;
Of course, I shall not have the time in the few minutes allotted to me to talk about our three major transportation modes. I shall therefore speak only about the Canadian National and VIA Rail in the province of Quebec, as I am convinced that hon. members from other provinces can plead their own case easily. Mr. Speaker, in April 1977 we learned that the Canadian National had finally made its first profits in 20 years for the operating year 1976. In its annual report, the Canadian National said that it was optimistic about the future profitability of its business. When the CN management talk about profitability, I always hope they make the distinction between the transport of goods and the transport of passengers. The same report states that the profits of $11.8 million compared with the deficit of $16.4 million in 1975 are attributable to the vitality brought about by re-organizing the company in six operational divisions. It should perhaps be added that more vigorous marketing and the impact of the technological advances of recent years also contributed to this surplus.
We must now look to the future. We must analyse carefully what the future holds since the CN notes that manpower and equipment expenditures will continue to cause problems for some time. The solution suggested by the CN to solve future problems would be to restrict expenditures and boost productivity by increasing rates if need be and maintaining the user pay concept. It is not on this point that we disagree, Mr. Speaker.
We of the Social Credit Party of Canada have always told the government-and we believe this more than ever-that the major cause of deficit is the continuing increase in interest
April 25, 1978

costs. Then, there is the multiplication of positions at the senior executive level and in all the bureaucratic sectors which are not profitable for the CN. The major cause of the CN deficit is the millions of dollars the company must pay each year for interest on the old accumulated debt and which would not exist if we had a logical financial system. The second cause is personnel that I consider unprofitable for the CN: to many employees behind desks and too few along the tracks to ensure adequate and permanent maintenance of the lines. In the past there were four linemen and one foreman for each eight or ten miles of track. Today two linemen cover 25 or 30 miles of track with three foremen, verificators, inspectors, whatever you want to call them. No wonder then we have so many derailments, which are very costly to the government and are due to a lack of maintenance personnel not to mention the fact that the trains are too long for the capacity of the tracks.
Regarding this subject, I wish to remind the House of the motion moved on November 28, 1974 by the member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) calling for a royal inquiry commission on national railways safety. This inquiry has still to come and we still witness a doubling in size of the bureaucratic supervisory staff. Let us add to that the overcentralization taking place in Montreal for rolling stock maintenance. I have already mentioned that to the House and nothing has changed since because management keep having their coffee breaks in the comfort of their offices while the army of inspectors drive around in cars; they no longer dare ride in trains and, besides, all their expenses are paid for.
I can believe the report when it says that wages will continue to be an element of the over-all deficit, Mr. Speaker. There are too many senior officials who do not really earn their fat salaries, too few maintenance employees who can barely make ends meet. That is the real tragedy of the CN.
So long as we fail to eradicate the evil at its root, we cannot expect to get cost efficient transportation. How come, I ask you, the CP keeps on showing enormous profits while the CN has recorded nothing but deficits over the past twenty years? Is it due to the competence of the former and the incompetence of the latter? I do not think so, Mr. Speaker. The blame for all that rests squarely on our transportation policy which is solely geared to the cost-efficiency factor first; we are trying to achieve that by excessively inflating the higher echelons of that organization to a point where we actually lose track of its very foundation. In other words, the CN is a clear case of overplanning in the skies while forgetting the fact that the CN is still running down on earth. Could it be also that there is a conflict of interest within the CN management? I am seriously asking myself this question when I notice that some CN managers are also shareholders of or even belong to the CP board of directors.
Mr. Speaker, when someone's interest is outside his home, there are many chances he will neglect his own family by providing certain little advantages to his associates on the
Transportation
outside. How come the CP retains the best roads while enjoying the same financial benefits as the CN which has to serve locations where the CP refuses to go because they are not profitable? The whole population is seriously wondering about it. Most of the important producers of paper, lumber and other commodities such as grains are now complaining about a shortage of railways cars.
Mr. Speaker, for too long the Canadian National has invested billions of dollars in hotel construction, forgetting completely to renew and improve its rolling stock. Today we suffer from the disastrous effects of such an attitude. If the western provinces are complaining, I urge them to visit the province of Quebec where we are 20 years behind.
I think I have said enough about freight trains. I wish now to add a few comments on passenger transportation and more specifically on our new company called VIA Rail. I take this opportunity to salute the first president of VIA Rail, Mr. John Roberts, whom I had the pleasure to meet. I wish to tell him that we from the province of Quebec are expecting much from that new company under his direction and more specifically my area of Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean where I have been fighting in the last 15 years to obtain better passenger service.
Mr. Speaker, in recent years we have witnessed the closing of railway stations, public disenchantment caused by an unacceptable service to the extent that we were wondering if those responsible at the time had not sworn to abolish our only rail service between Montreal, Dolbeau and Chicoutimi. They even proposed an impossible day schedule that would be a disincentive to customers because of the late arrival time in Montreal. On February 28, 1977, I proposed a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43 on that matter that read as follows:
Whereas according to the new CN passenger service schedule becoming effective in early April, the only passenger train will be arriving into Montreal at
23:30.
-in the night-
Whereas at that late hour all connections with other trains is impossible.
Whereas according to that new schedule, three days and two nights will be needed to spend one business day in Montreal, that waste of time never having existed previously because the same trip is now made during the night; the implementation of that new schedule will cause serious prejudice to the travelling public in the area to the extent where the clientele will disappear,
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi: That the Minister of Transport exert immediately the required pressures with the CN president and Mr. Jean-Marie Beaulieu, general superintendent, to delay the implementation of the new schedule for six months, with a view to allowing local organizations to present their suggestions in that regard.
On April 4, 1977, I received the reply of the CN which reads as follows, and I quote:
You must have received a letter from Mr. Levasseur, advising you-
I shall spare you the opening paragraph of the letter in which I am thanked for the two letters I sent, one dated February 25, the other March 1.

April 25, 1978
Transportation
You must have received a letter from Mr. Levasseur advising you that we have decided to keep the night train in service. Besides, on Friday, I sent a press release to the newspapers saying among other things: "The Montreal-Chicoutimi and Quebec-Senneterre-Cochrane night trains will be kept in service in both directions after April 24, contrary to what had been previously announced. The decision to substitute day trains for them has therefore been suspended pending further notice, and the present schedule will apply except for a few minor details".
Mr. Speaker, I refer to this specific case. I would have some twenty others because I have a very thick file on this question but I will spare the House because time does not allow me to read more.
I would like to read an article published in the newspaper La Presse of Montreal of June 2, 1977. It is about VIA Rail integration with other modes of transport. I quote:
While trying to revive in the mind of the public the use of the train as a mode of mass transport, VIA Rail Canada does not intend to work in an ivory tower. On the contrary, it wants to combine its services with other modes of passenger transport in use in this country.
That is the essence of a speech made by Mr. John Roberts ... in March 1977. The basic objective of VIA Rail, Mr. Roberts said, will be to provide high quality service suited to the real needs of Canadians. The tariff structure will have to help make it attractive while ensuring its viability from an economic standpoint.
Mr. Roberts recognizes that railway transportation has been clearly neglected and said that for about a quarter of a century, 95 per cent of federal expenditures for human transportation have gone to aviation and the road infrastructure. But, he says, the mistake of neglecting railway transportation has been recognized, and VIA Rail is precisely one of the means to correct it.
However, any attempt by VIA Rail to develop without taking into consideration the other modes of transport would serve to give official recognition to the fact that what Mr. Roberts calls comprehensive national planning has been neglected. Hence VIA Rail's desire to combine with other passenger services.
Talking about that planning, Mr. Speaker, when in today's motion, the government is being asked to take action to clarify the mandate, paragraph (c) of the motion says about that planning: to clarify the mandate of the Canadian Transport Commission to ensure that the regional diversity of the country is taken into consideration in all decisions of the commission. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether the CTC from now on will play its true role. I think that in the final analysis it has already started to play its true role based on the invitation they sent us recently. I would like to quote that invitation which reads as follows:
Find attached to this letter an order of the Railway Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission advising you that public hearings will be held on dates and places yet to be determined concerning trains No. 170, 171, 172, etc., between Quebec City (Sainte-Foy) and Chicoutimi; Montreal and Chicoutimi; Chambord and Dolbeau; and Quebec City (Limoilou) and Rivierc-a-Pierre...
The commission thus informs you in advance so you will have more time to decide whether you will be making representations and to prepare and submit those representations if you feel that you are a person, corporation or public body interested or likely to be affected.
While reading this, I cannot help wondering if this notice has indeed been sent to all Quebec municipalities, as I had suggested to the department, and to all Quebec towns, chambers of commerce and social organizations to advise them that

such a survey would be carried out, because for many years now we have been urging the CN to consult the public. I think this is the first time we receive such an invitation, and I should like to mention here that the commission should send similar invitations to all public organizations involved which must use the railroads.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that the time I have is coming to an end, and I still have something to say about transportation in the province of Quebec. I limited my remarks to my own region, because I had something to say on behalf of my region, but I suggest there remains a lot to be said about the shortcomings of the passenger service throughout the province, in Abitibi as well as in the Gaspe area. I think that the consultations which the Canadian Transport Commission intends to hold will prove useful throughout the province, and we expect a lot from them.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks by stating to the House that I want to speak on the entire question of the grain industry and the movement of agricultural products out of western Canada, as well as on some of the things which have taken place under the aegis of the present government.
While listening to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) this afternoon, one thing Canadians must remember is that the present government has been in power since the early 1960's. The government has to accept the blame for what has transpired during that particular time. It cannot wash its hands of any past problems, and just look to the future. The government cannot indicate that it is sorry things are the way they are, and not provide any real solutions.
We must look at what has transpired since the 1974 election and the promises which were made at that time. We will draw the conclusion that very little has happened in terms of over-all transportation in western Canada. Some studies have been conducted, and a few recommendations have been implemented in connection with those studies. I give the government and the minister their dues, but very little concrete results have transpired.
Over the years the government has regulated rates in a fashion which has inhibited economic growth in the prairies, certainly from the point of view of processing and secondary manufacturing. It has allowed the entire rail system in western Canada to deteriorate to the point where it is struggling to keep up with exports at the present time. As a result of this deterioration and mismanagement, which has squandered millions of tax dollars, the government finally was forced into doing something. On April 19, 1975, the Minister of Transport announced the formation of the Hall commission to look at the entire situation of grain transportation in western Canada.
The Hall report was tabled in the House of Commons in May 1977. It contains some 92 major recommendations, ranging in scope from branch line abandonment, freight rates, to port facilities. It is a very comprehensive and carefully thought
April 25, 1978

out report, designed basically to bring back some sanity to the system, and to attempt to implement the principles that form the basis of the original Crow rate agreement, which is adhered to in western Canada at the present time.
Nearly one year after the publication of this report, the government's response virtually has been to ignore most of the recommendations and the provisions in it. Of the 92 recommendations by Mr. Justice Hall, the government has acted fully on only seven. Another three have been implemented partially, and 24 others have prompted statements to the effect that they wil be studied further. Better than two-thirds of those recommendations have never been acknowledged by the government. Neither the minister nor his senior staff have undertaken to meet with Mr. Justice Hall to discuss his very, very important report. In fact, it is one of the most important reports to ever come out of western Canada.
The minister has so far refused to act upon one of the most important recommendations in the Hall report. I am referring to the recommendation which dealt with the freight rate structure and the principles upon which it is based. I should like to refer to page 534 of the Hall report, where Mr. Justice Hall is reported as saying the following:
The production and processing of agricultural products should take place in the regions of this country which have a natural geographical advantage for such activities. Freight rates and other transport related policies should not destroy nor hinder these natural advantages.
It continues:
The flour milling industry in Canada be permitted to enjoy the natural geographic advantage of locating in western Canada.
Virtually this recommendation is repeated word for word later in the report dealing with the rapeseed crushing industry, the livestock processing industry, and the malting industry. Each of these industries would be encouraged to locate in the west to be near the producers of their basic raw materials, if the government's transportation policies effectively did not bar them from being cost effective. In many cases it is the inequities of the freight rate structure which prevent these industries from providing the prairies with needed jobs and the foundation for a healthy economy.
In the area of livestock, one example came to a head in 1976. In that year Alberta effectively lost one of its most thriving industries, hog production. There were many reasons for this loss which left over 8,000 hog farms idle in Alberta, but one of those reasons is surprisingly simple but nevertheless tragic. It is cheaper to ship 800 pounds of feed grain to eastern Canada on which to raise a pig to shipping weight, than it is to ship the 150 pounds of pork which the pig produces. At the present time, Alberta imports a substantial amount of pork products from the United States, and ships pig feed to eastern Canada. Nowhere else in the world is there a country which grows its feed in one region and raises its livestock in another.
Similar situations exist in other sectors which were mentioned by Mr. Justice Hall. As a result of stop-off charges and discriminatory interest and storage charges, it is cheaper to ship wheat east to be milled and import the flour, than it is to produce the flour in the prairies. Similarly, these problems
Transportation
exist in respect of the malting industry. I should like to quote from the report once again, which reads as follows:
Freight rates on malting barley continue on the statutory basis, and apply to both the malting barley and barley malt.
I emphasize that because one is raw material and the other is processed product. One of the clearest examples of the inequities in the government's transportation policy, if such a policy exists in any recognizable form, can be provided by referring to the case of the rapeseed industry. If ever there was an industry which enjoyed a locational advantage, it should be oilseed production. But that is not the case, in spite of the fact this crop is not really grown outside the prairies.
As recently as 1974 the Rapeseed Association of Canada was looking to the future with bright expectations. However, the rapeseed crushing industry in the prairies was not able to develop as fully as it might, because, once again, it was cheaper to ship the raw material to eastern and foreign markets than it was to ship the finished product, in spite of the substantial reduction in volume. By 1976 producers and processors alike were expressing serious concern about the future of the oilseed crushing industry in the prairies, and the origins of the problem can be traced simply to the fact that the Crow rate applied to the bulk shipment of rapeseed and not to the finished oil product. This fact makes it more economic to export seed than oil or meal, but at the same time thousands of jobs that belong in western Canada are being filled instead by workers in Japanese crushing plants. The federal government has stepped in with an interim subsidy program, but it is not good enough.
A recently published study of the effects of the Crow rate structure on the rapeseed industry by a group of economists in Saskatchewan concluded that the low Crowsnest rate and a high Japanese import tariff were holding back the rapeseed processing industry in western Canada. As partial relief in this area, however, the government would be well advised to take heed of Justice Hall's recommendation at page 536 of his report, namely, that the federal department of transportation and communications devote more effort to export market development for rapeseed meal and oil.
Nevertheless, at least one half of the problem is directly associated with the freight rate inequities between processed oil and meal and the unprocessed seed. The ideal situation would be an extension of the Crow rate to cover processed oil and meal combined with an elimination of the Japanese tariff. Hopefully the tariff question will be settled at the current round of GATT negotiations.
However, the study concluded, using 1974 figures, that if the tariff were maintained and only the Crow rate extended to cover oil and meal, the advantages :o producers, processors and westerners in general would have been substantial in 1974. Rapessed oil consumers would have paid approximately $1.3 million more for the product. To offset that, crusher earnings would have risen an extra $907,000; grower earnings would have increased by some $3 million; the rapessed meal consum-

April 25, 1978
Transportation
er would have paid nearly $900,000 less; and our foreign exchange earnings would have have risen by a dramatic $3.6 million. This represents a clear benefit of some $7 million but, more importantly, it provides support for the development of an industry natural to the prairie provinces-one that would provide needed jobs and contribute to the evolution of a stable western economy, which in turn would go a long way towards overcoming western dissatisfaction and what is commonly known as western alienation.
The Hall report dealt with a broad range of specifics and general problems relating to grain handling and transportation in the west. It demonstrated two overriding facts. The first is that the grain handling system has deteriorated immensely as a result of this government's misguided attempts at policy formulation. The second relates in many ways to the first, and putting it simply, this sorry excuse for a management team has not been able to devise a national transportation policy which allows for the development of an industrial base and a market system which would promote the processing of agricultural products in the west.
On this side of the House we have continually asserted the need for a rational transportation policy which would support and encourage regional development priorities. We have continually argued that since transportation is one of the most heavily subsidized industries in our economy, the Canadian people are entitled to a meaningful return on their substantial tax dollar investment. That return should be in the form of new and expanded industries which are based on the particular geographical, social and cultural advantages of our various regions.
Our transportation system should be a tool which will help us to build a stronger, healthier and more united Canada. Neither government regulations nor administration of our transportation system should result in road blocks which are placed in the way of progress, but this is exactly what is happening time and time again when one looks at western Canada. The government has allowed the grain transportation system to deteriorate to a point where it threatens the very livelihood of the prairie grain producer, and when it threatens that group it threatens the foundation of the prairie society and, in fact, has a certain spin-off effect on the entire nation.
This government's failure to act in any comprehensive or meaningful way with regard to the over-all transportation system in the west has produced chaos which has significantly retarded growth in the prairies and even in those areas which enjoy a natural advantage. We are at the point at the present time-certainly all of the blame cannot be laid on the transportation system, but it has a great deal to do with it-where we are going to be owing over $12 million in demurrage charges that will ultimately be paid by the farmers in western Canada. The demurrage is there because the grain cannot be moved to the Vancouver port in time to load the particular boats that are waiting.
With the exception of the expansion at Prince Rupert, not one of the seven fully implemented proposals involved any significant expenditures, although some reorganization is
[Mr. Murta.l
implied. The minister has done a good job of undermining the original effectiveness of these proposals. Instead of the prairie rail authority recommended by Justice Hall, for example, we have the Prairie Rail Action Committee, which is a watered down version of the Prairie Rail Authority, and is not what we on this side of the House would have liked to have had. The minister has not moved to implement Justice Hall's recommendation that the railways be compensated for the cost of moving grain by rail. As a result, the responsibility for maintenance and upgrading of those lines already in the network and those to be added still rests with the government through its branch line subsidy.
Shortly after the release of the Hall report, one of the minister's frequent press releases stated that he intended to encourage branch line rehabilitation with an initial "firm commitment of $200 million." This was less than one half of the $450 million recommended by Justice Hall in his report. To compound the confusion, it was not long before the minister had cut the $200 million in half, leaving $100 million earmarked for 1978. During the cabinet's recent roadshow to western Canada, the minister announced that $75 million would be made available for branch line improvement in 1979. So the amounts of money are certainly dropping, and this still does not add up to the minister's firm commitment of some $200 million. In fact, it represents a decrease from that recommended by Justice Hall.
More significantly, the branch line subsidy just is not working. The railroads are receiving too much of the taxpayers' dollars without having to account for the way in which those dollars are spent. The railroads really have the best of both worlds-subsidies plus grants to be spent as they wish. But not one cent of branch line subsidy in recent years has been spent on upgrading branch lines in western Canada.
We on this side believe, with Mr. Justice Hall, that the railroads must be compensated for the difference between the cost of transporting grain and the statutory rates. But then they must be responsible for retaining and upgrading the prairie rail network without further subsidy from Canadian taxpayers.
There is much more I could say about the inequities which have existed over the years and which still exist. They predominate in the minds of many westerners who seek a natural advantage in terms not only of growing the product, which they do so well, but also the processing of that product and shipping it to other parts of North America and the world.
The government must realize that secondary manufacturing is needed very badly in western Canada. Without it we will have alienation and frustration. Proper transportation policies would be a way to alleviate this very troublesome aspect of life in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to note that the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) agrees that the present branch line subsidy program
April 25, 1978

that has been in effect for a number of years by virtue of the National Transportation Act passed in 1967 has not really worked. The railroads have taken the money and put it into general operating revenue, but they have not applied it to upgrading the various lines for which the funds were paid. That is one of the reasons for the government's policy-to make sure that a work program in connection with the rehabilitation spending is applied to specific lines. It is for that purpose alone that federal funds go to the railroads. That is one point on which we can agree with the hon. member.
I am sure the hon. member for Lisgar knows very well that the problems he alluded to in his remarks regarding the pork industry in Alberta, the beef industry in western Canada, flour milling, meat packing, rapeseed crushing and other related processing industry problems, are not solely the result of transportation policy or lack of it. Things are a great deal more complex than that. Since we have an 1897 rate that has not been adjusted for the last few years for the raw product, while the other rates have been allowed to change and adapt to the rate of inflation, it is obvious that there will be problems. As usual, my hon. friend opposite did not offer any concrete solutions.
This government shares his concern but I think we have made real progress in implementing the thrust of the Hall Commission report on these and other major issues of importance to western Canada.
The motion before us seeks to keep alive a number of the myths that the opposition continue to propagate in regard to transportation policy. My hon. friend opposite, who is my neighbouring member in the province of Alberta as well as opposition critic and whom I consider to be an excellent member, very knowledgeable about transportation, said some things today that no doubt were due to the over-zealous writing of his caucus research staff. He spoke of the lack of effort by the government in this part of the country. Mr. Speaker, he knows full well that this government has made more progress in the last three or four years than any government in the history of the country in addressing some of the very real problems of Canadian transportation policy.
Dozens of examples can be cited to demonstrate the efforts of the government and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in that respect. There are the selective freight subsidies paid on commodities moving in and out of the maritimes. These have been worked out with people in the maritimes and have evolved as a result of policies brought forward three or four years ago. Committees of transport ministers exist in the maritimes, western Canada, Quebec and Ontario. The hon. member said he was in favour of approaching these problems on a regional basis. That is what the present federal and provincial committees do-they recognize regional differences. Support is given to ferry services on the east coast and the west coast; air facilities have been improved and expanded; we have developed not only a fully consultative mechanism but a new ports policy, and new container terminals are operating, are under way or have been announced in practically every part of
Transportation
the country. Improvements have been made and issues addressed.
The question of passenger rail service was raised in this House yesterday and again today in this debate. Highway agreements have been developed and are in operation across the country. There are two or three in western Canada. There is the highway strengthening program for the prairie provinces with over $20 million paid to the province of Saskatchewan, more than that to Alberta and a similar amount to Manitoba. The money is given by the federal government at the request of and with the co-operation of the provinces to upgrade the standard of highways so that load limits can be raised and made uniform from British Columbia to Ontario. This will allow highway transportation to develop with greater uniformity across the country.
Another agreement which is of particular interest to me and other members from western Canada is the western northlands agreement. I am sure that hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) will be familiar with that in general. An agreement has been signed with each of the three western provinces. An interim agreement has been completed with Saskatchewan for an expenditure of $35.6 million for transportation, roads and community access roads in northern Saskatchewan. There is a similar program in Alberta and a larger, more comprehensive program in a long term agreement with Manitoba. These are specific and concrete examples of programs designed to meet regional needs in this country which have been enunciated by members of parliament, provincial spokesmen and other interested groups.
There has been a real need to develop transportation networks and links into isolated communities in Saskatchewan. There was a contribution of $9 million odd dollars in federal funds to Highway No. 2 from Montreal Lake to Lake La Ronge, $2.3 million for Highway No. 155 from Green Lake to Beauval, and $5 million for Highway No. 135 in the Creighton area. These communities have existed in the north for a long time, are out of the main stream, and have been brought in by these programs. The community access road to Stanley Mission, the oldest community in Saskatchewan, received $1.7 million. A community access road was constructed there last year for the first time in its history. Similar programs have been operated throughout a dozen communities across Saskatchewan, including even airstrips.
Toward the end of the remarks made by my hon. friend, the hon. member for Vegreville, he elaborated to some extent on the platform of the Progressive Conservative opposition. As usual that party is anxious to implement the Hall report, being very careful to be non-specific about that, not to spell out what they are going to do and when.
You will hear about it.

Secondly, they are anxious to make use of transportation as a tool in rectifying or remedying regional disparities in this country. This is exactly what this govern-
4858

April 25, 1978
Transportation
ment has been doing, and it has been succeeding to a much greater degree than has ever been the case before.
If I heard my hon. friend correctly, his party would modify the CTC to establish a western arm, as the minister has already announced. My hon. friend was good enough to enlarge on that by saying that he would like a maritimes arm as well. That is a good concept and he will have no argument from the government in that respect. But, again it is policy which has been announced by this government and by the present Minister of Transport.
The opposition are talking about a huge infusion of funds that will be required. As one listened to the hon. member for Lisgar, particularly it appears it will be a very large infusion. I believe fiscal policy was also mentioned. I am not sure if my hon. friend was here, I think he was, but in the last budget a new policy was introduced providing for a faster write-off of railroad equipment. This is designed to encourage railroad rehabilitation and an updating program which this government has already embarked upon.
Five to ten years too late.

After nine years of study by the Progressive Conservative commission of years ago, that still has to be their record in transportation. That is all we can compare it to. We have nothing more than that rusty old record of that royal commission dealing with transportation from the last Conservative government of this country. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians both from the east and the west will be looking at that record of theirs as opposed to the record of this government in the field of transportation in the various areas that have been dealt with.
I had to smile at a point made by my hon. friend. The Conservatives wish to generate an attitude of trust and confidence. That has to be a first. That is the one I could certainly endorse. In my short time here, and elsewhere in public life, I have seen the Conservatives excel at generating an attitude of mistrust across this country, whether it concerns transportation or any other issue. I was pleased to hear my hon. friend from Vegreville say that they wished to generate an attitude of trust and confidence. I am sure he would want to see that happen; he has the opportunity to begin now.
He could have begun sooner to implement and generate trust and confidence from one end of this country to the other. That certainly has not been demonstrated in transportation policy, grain policy, fiscal policy, tax policy or any other subject or field one might examine, if one listened to the remarks made inside and outside of this House over the last couple of months. So that is a very welcome change.
I think it is worth noting for the record the achievements of this government with respect to implementing the Hall commission report. I would remind my hon. friend opposite that it was this government, the Department of Transport and the present minister, when he was minister in charge of the grains group and the Canadian Wheat Board, which established the Hall commission to look at and deal with the whole complex question of improvements in the grain handling system of

western Canada. That commission did an excellent job throughout western Canada and elsewhere in looking at and assessing the problems and making recommendations. The commission did a great deal to allay the fears and concerns which have been there, and genuinely so, for many years.
What did the government do upon receiving the Hall commission report? Within 11 days-and this has to be something of a record for any government, be it a municipal government, provincial government or otherwise-an order in council had been passed which added 1,813 miles of prairie rail lines. This addition was recommended by the Hall commission to the basic rail network. It increased the total to some 14,000 miles, which was about three-quarters of all prairie rail trackage. In other words, there was no more fear or apprehension about abandonment, of elevators being closed or lines closed, over three-quarters of the prairie network. That was accomplished within 11 days. That certainly has to be the main thrust of that report.
Another 2,344 miles that were suggested should be transferred to the jurisdiction of a prairie rail authority were protected from abandonment until January 1, 1979. Again that portion of the rail lines examined by the Hall commission and sort of left in limbo was set over until such time as it could be assessed, looked at and categorized one way or the other into a permanent network or abandoned.
The question of prairie branch line rehabilitation has been alluded to by both of the hon. members opposite and by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) as being something which is still a long way off. There is evidence that work has proceeded on a number of rail lines right now in the prairie area and money has been budgeted. The work program is lined up.
Perhaps it might be worth putting on the record of the House of Commons some of the projects that are either under way or scheduled for this particular year. They are: Swan River to Sturgis; Delisle to Beechy; Delisle to Dunblane; Dunblane to Elrose; Glidden to Alsask. I have about four or five pages of these projects covering every part of the three prairie provinces. Vegreville, Alberta, is mentioned; the hon. member referred to problems there. There is another line going out of Vegreville that is scheduled for revamping or new ties. There is another one out of Lloydminster into Alberta which is scheduled for new ties this year. Both the lines from Kerrobert to Rosetown and Lloydminster to Wilkie involve new ties and renovations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member still has three minutes left of his allotted time. I suggest that we do not see the clock for that three minutes. We could allow the hon. member that time and then give the floor to the next speaker and call it six o'clock. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few brief comments in conclusion. The NDP spokesman today, along with other representatives of his party, will have to devise a new
April 25, 1978

version of a transportation policy for western Canada. For the last good number of years their sole policy in transportation has revolved around the fears and apprehensions of massive rail abandonments across the prairies. The implementation of the Hall commission report and the study itself has put the rest those old fears that have been developed and fanned by harangues from many an NDP spokesman, both federal and provincial, over the years.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre in this debate today resorted to a good ploy from his own point of view; he expressed concern for the line in his own area. There are some lines where there has been and will be abandonment. Above all, there are many lines, many communities over the prairie provinces today, by far the majority of the total geography affected by rail lines, where that uncertainty has been cleared away. There is no longer any uncertainty. That has been the most positive achievement of the Hall commission in my opinion and, indeed, of this government in dealing with that particular question, plus the major commitment to rebuild, upgrade and renovate the entire branch line network.
That is a major beginning and a major part of any transportation improvements in the entire grain handling network, to go along with the various other things that I am sure other hon. members will be referring to in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to listen to the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) as he outlined the progress, so-called, in the west in the field of transportation. He had the courage, or lack of it, to venture into the Atlantic provinces and tell us how good they had been to him. But, Mr. Speaker, he never rode the rails from Port aux Basques to St. John's, Newfoundland. He never got on the ferry from Cape Breton to Newfoundland. He is not aware that there was a time when the government regulated transportation in such a way that it was possible to ship steel from Sydney pretty well across Canada and make money at it; that there was a time when we could ship a number of products from the maritimes to central
Transportation
Canada. That was the good old time. Nowadays freight rates are so high that we have been obliged to seek other markets.
There is no need to review the position of the steel company on Cape Breton Island to find out how it is doing under this government, because that is done on a regular basis in the House. Among the reasons which have led to the affairs of this company being in very serious shape, along with others, is the level of rates which have been imposed. Contrary to the intention when confederation was entered into, rates have been imposed which have precluded the maritime provinces from the Canadian market.
The hon. member spoke at some length about the moneys the central government had provided to the provinces. But he did not tell the whole story, and unless people read other contributions to this debate they will be seriously misled. What the hon. member did not say was that every time the minister held a lollipop out to the provinces what he said to them, in effect, was: "You can have it if you put another one with it, but if you don't have another lollipop you won't get this one".
One might, for instance, review the $100 million or the $130 million-I was not quite clear as to the amount when he had done garbling it out-which he proposed to give to the Atlantic provinces toward the rationalization of transport services. But when the provinces began to deal with the minister they found the terms were extremely expensive. They found that he would not give the Atlantic provinces anything unless they matched it.
In the field of transportation, and particularly as it relates to highways, on which most of this money will be spent, the Government of Canada was in the habit of offering to provinces in eastern Canada and in certain cases in western Canada a 90-10 federal-provincial program or an 80-20 federal-provincial program; but when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) started to deal it out, he dealt it out to the provinces on a 50-50 basis, and he said, "If you have another lollipop to go with this one, we will give you the one we have, but under our terms and conditions".
This means that by the time a province buys a right-of-way to build certain highway connections which are necessary, under this program the province will spend $60 for every $40 spent by the federal government. I submit that if this Santa Claus pulled off his mask, Jekyll and Hyde would be revealed. The minister did not tell us that the railroad on Prince Edward Island has got to such a state that it is doubtful if five years from now there will be trains moving on it. I am not aware of any grant-and I am sure the minister did not miss any- which is going to be given to P.E.I. to recondition that rail service.
The minister sounded as if he was going through a batch of Liberal promises to local constituents. He sounded as if he was trying to save his own conscience, sweeten the disposition of those scattered across the prairies and other parts of Canada and cajole them into voting for his party. However, when you start describing a situation in which you are putting in new
