ties, you are talking about railroad maintenance, and that goes on every month of every year under every government. The minister certainly got down to the nit-picking level when he started to brag about that.
The transportation structure as it exists in Canada has been getting some attention as election year approaches. Whether the election is this year or next only one man knows, but as it approaches there are ad hoc solutions to the transportation problems of Canada. Some specific problems have been attacked, but basically it has been an ad hoc program without rationalization. The government has chosen to buy many rail cars for the west. I do not quarrel with that, if that is the right approach, but why has there not been a rationalized program to examine equipment shortages which exist across Canada and not just in the area of Canada in which the minister lives? That is not good enough.
I would like to cite another example to which perhaps the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley should have paid a little attention. The minister has been giving much attention to the new ports policy. The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley said that the government is looking at the east and the west and having meetings here and there, but what happened? All at once the east and the west met without the minister, and they found that the minister had gone to the west and said that the eastern provinces agreed with the government's ports policy. When the east got out west and heard what the west had to say, the east found that there were ten provinces in Canada, none of which agreed with the ports package.
They all disagreed with it because they felt that they should have a voice in their own destinies with regard to the ports of Canada. They pleaded with the minister to be represented on the various ports boards which would be appointed, and he said no. The premiers of Atlantic Canada then sent a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) telling him that they wanted to be represented on the boards which are to be appointed and to have a say in the management of the ports of eastern Canada, but the Prime Minister said no.
The destiny of Canada and of particular provinces rests with the decision-making process with regard to ports policy, and the provinces will have no say. The provinces have had no say about rates and little, if any, about VIA Rail. There has been practically no consultation, but much dictating, with respect to expenditures of so-called joint moneys by Ottawa, and we just do not have a transportation policy. This government has not been capable of analyzing either the needs of shippers or the capabilities of carriers.
Does the government know that when a certain commodity group met with the railroads it found that it took 24 to 28 days for a round trip of less than 500 miles for one car? Why should the Government of Canada buy cars for a railroad which cannot make a round trip of 500 miles in less than 24 to 28 days for one car? Why should the government buy cars to transport any commodity when a railroad as a competitor takes 18 to 20 days for a 400 mile round trip journey for one car? If we buy cars for this outfit, we are buying cars for the outfit to park without knowing the substance of the problem

with which we are trying to deal. We are trying to deal with it from the wrong end. Under this man's policy we do not know what it costs the railroads to carry a car of potatoes from Prince Edward Island, a car of fish from Newfoundland or a car of wood pulp from New Brunswick to any destination.
If the minister has this information, it is secret and will not be divulged. These questions have been asked in the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, but we in Atlantic Canada do not know whether we are being charged what the tariff will bear or a fair rate; and neither does anybody else in Canada because the CPR does not have to account, as Bell Canada does. The CNR does not have to account for its charges, as does NB Tel. We pour subsidies into an operation, the mechanics of which we do not understand. That is not a policy. There has to be service, and at the moment we are not getting it.
I remind the House that we have been having problems at the port of Saint John. The only way the ports of Saint John and Halifax can be expanded is if the provinces and municipalities put money into federal works which they will never own. The provinces will never own them, but they have to put money in. I do not want to be misunderstood by any member of this House. I do not begrudge the St. Lawrence Valley the policy that the Government of Canada is exercising, but I want the same policy in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland.
Hear, hear!

The government is selecting its political plums and spending its money in an unjust fashion, which brings about disunity in this nation. That is discrimination of the rankest kind. We are talking about the CNR and its recapitalization. We are going to double track through the Rockies, fix tracks across the prairies and examine tracks from Quebec City to Windsor; but when the president was asked what is scheduled for the maritime provinces, he said that everything is great down there and that we do not need anything in Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, New Brunswick or Nova Scotia. He told us there are no plans for that area.
That is the policy which the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley praised to the sky. That is the Santa Claus of the Jekyll and Hyde type. When the minister wears his beard, he is the true Santa; but when he pulls off his beard, we see the other discriminatory personality. That is typical of this government.
There is another matter which must be rationalized. We must operate on a competitive basis. Let me give an example. In the last five years the freight rate on grains from Thunder Bay to Woodstock, Ontario, has gone up 30 per cent. Members opposite from Quebec should be interested in this. I think they were present when it was discussed. To Sherbrooke, Quebec, it has gone 80 per cent, and to Moncton, New Brunswick, it has gone 90 per cent. And this from the minister who claims he has a transportation policy for Canada! When the rates from Thunder Bay to Woodstock, Ontario, are raised up to 30 per cent and from Thunder Bay to Moncton up to 90 per cent, is
April 25, 1978

that a good transportation policy for this country? It is discrimination, lack of judgment and lack of understanding. I suggest it is ignorance of the things that are going on.
In the Atlantic area we have a regional air carrier which served in good faith points which were not economically viable on the advice of and with aid and direction from the government. They were assured that a certain subsidy would be paid them if they would serve these particular points of interest to the Government of Canada, and to all of Canada for that matter. What did they find? Inflation came along, the subsidy remained constant, there was no indexing of it, no increment in it, the company lost money. On top of this there was lack of rationalization again, because in those routes which were then profitable for Eastern Provincial Airways, Air Canada paralleled and inconvenienced them. They did everything they could to take the business away from them.
It is no use improving the tracks in the prairies, it is no use improving the tracks from Quebec to Windsor, and it is no use improving the tracks from Quebec to Saint John, for that matter, if you do not understand the problem. What is wrong with this government's transportation structure is that they do not understand the problem, and I want to tell the House why. You cannot approach a subject as complex, complicated and meaningful to all of Canada as is transportation to this country, by pulling people out of a hat or from the Prime Minister's office to lay down policies for Atlantic Canada, how much subsidies you will give to the prairie provinces, and say that this should be a good plum for this area or that area, and it should make them happy politically so they will vote for you. Whether it is land, sea or air transportation, there must be rationalization.
For example, you cannot have recapitalization of the CNR when it can be established, in spite of evidence which was presented to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, that the trucking companies owned by CNR are getting advantages in the piggyback service which are not extended to their competitors. This can be established, contrary to the evidence which was given. I do not think we should recapitalize that structure until we are guaranteed in an unqualified way that the competitive structures will not be placed in a position of disadvantage because we forgive the debt of $808 million to the CNR.
I have to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not believe there is anybody in the House at present who, in spite of the Hall report, the work which the committees have done and the time which the minister and other hon. members have spent, really knows just how a proper transportation program from eastern Canada to western Canada and all the points in between can be put in place. But I can tell you that we are not shipping lumber products out of New Brunswick by Canadian National Railways; we are trucking them from the mills to the U.S. railroad companies, which are taking them to markets in New England and farther down into the states because our rails, which are beside the mills, have a subsidiary just across the
Transportation
border which will take the products to the New England states and to other American points at a price that is lower than the price at the mill, a price that is so much lower that you can truck them to a main point and put it aboard the U.S. railroad.
I said this in the House on another occasion and somebody across the floor yelled that the U.S. railways are subsidized so they can do this. Let me point out that Mr. Bandeen, president of CNR which owns three subsidiaries in the United States, told the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications that he is not aware that any of his subsidiaries are receiving any subsidies whatsoever for the normal service which they provide in the United States. So this shoots down that balloon.
Atlantic Canada wants to know why rates in Atlantic Canada are not competitive with rates in Maine. We want to know why rates to Atlantic Canada have gone up by 90 per cent while they have gone up by only 30 per cent to Woodstock, Ontario. We want to know why, when you take the beard off Santa Claus, you find Jekyll and Hyde. We think we deserve a reasonable break in the ferry service to Newfoundland, for the transportation of potatoes to central Canadian and other markets and for the transportation of potatoes to export markets, for fair competition within the competitive structure in transportation which exists between rail and road, for an open policy, an open rate structure, a known quantity with which we can deal and with which we can come to an understanding. The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley should take off the blindfold and go back to the veterinary service which he understands so well and about which I know nothing.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite happy to follow my colleague the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), who has given us the down side of transport in Atlantic Canada. Possibly I can balance the record on that score for that particular region.
Hear, hear!
Bring back the Newfie Bullet.
We have new highways and new buses to replace the Newfie Bullet. The Newfie Bullets are on this side.
Bunch of duds!

I am quite happy to speak on this motion in one sense, but in another sense it seems to be a waste of debating time because this motion is quite erroneous as it applies to Atlantic Canada. I do not know if it is intended to apply to Atlantic Canada because I notice that towards the end it says:
... to implement the major recommendations of the Hall commission report on grain handling and transportation in the west.
A couple of studies have been carried out in the east also. I do not know if the opposition is aware of them, but they are certainly not mentioned iii the motion. If the opposition is concentrating on the west rather than on the Atlantic area,

April 25, 1978
Transportation
that is understandable because, after reading Charles Lynch's columns and having come back from the west, I know that there is a great need for the opposition parties to pay attention to the west. They certainly cannot take the west for granted and they need to come up with some policies for western Canada.
Yes, keep on listening to Charles Lynch.

I suggest to opposition members that they should start developing some policies for Atlantic Canada also.
I also want to point out what might be a pattern of development for such a policy. The motion states that the government failed to implement the promises of the 1974 election campaign. I invite opposition members to examine the Atlantic Liberal manifesto of the 1974 election campaign. I do not have it with me. Do you know why? I filed it away far back because we in Atlantic Canada know that it has been dealt with.
Empty promises.

Eighty per cent to 90 per cent of the commitments made in that Atlantic Liberal manifesto of the 1974 campaign have been dealt with. If hon. members opposite have a copy of it, I invite them to spread it around to their colleagues because the facts speak for themselves.
The second part of the motion refers to the abandonment of the user-pay concept and the development of transportation objectives which will enhance national harmony, reduce regional disparity and promote balanced economic growth. I want to set on the record some of the policies that this government has carried out in Atlantic Canada to achieve those aims and objectives. I will have to read because I cannot remember all the facts and figures. There are a myriad of them, and they are substantial. I want to refer to the government's record in transportation in Atlantic Canada.
Last year the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) announced a $125 million transportation program aimed at improving services and facilities over the next three years. Approximately $100 million will be spent by the federal government to improve highways in the four provinces. Only last week the federal government and the province of Newfoundland announced a formal agreement on a three-year $60 million highway improvement program in that province. We have been scored because it is 50/50 and not 90/10. How many 90/10 agreements can there be?
There is much to be done in Atlantic Canada. I do not think the federal government has been niggardly in its agreements in the past. In addition to the $60 million, which was formalized in Newfoundland last week, I suspect the total is something between $60 million and $70 million of DREE money which has gone into the establishment of trunk roads and major highway building programs in Newfoundland. If that is added together, the total amount is over $100 million in one province

alone, most of which was 90/10. That is a record the government can be proud of.
We have not built all the highways that should be built. I will not be satisfied until there is a highway across Labrador. Last week the Minister of Transport was in Labrador to talk about that very subject. I hope some funds are found in the future to aid the province of Newfoundland in carrying out that project. Is a 90/10 agreement user-pay? It is not. It is the taxpayers all across Canada providing the funds for the federal government to assist provinces which are less able to pay. It is not a user-pay concept. It is the spending of money on transportation in a region which needs it, without regard for the payback on the part of those using the transport system.
In addition to the highway program, there has been new airport construction at a total cost of $21 million. It will provide valuable links to areas at some distance from major New Brunswick and Newfoundland centres.
Is that pork-barrelling?
That is looking after transportation needs.
It sounds like pork-barrelling.
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) listened to all the other speeches. I suggest we listen to his.
Hear, hear!

Hon. members opposite do not want to hear the facts. They do not want to hear the truth. They want to preach doom and gloom. This new airport construction will provide for fast and efficient transport of equipment and supplies to valuable resource areas in New Brunswick. In New Brunswick, $6.4 million will be spent over the next three years to complete the development of Charlo airport. A new airport at St. Leonard, on which work was already begun, will be built at a total cost of $3.8 million over the next two years. In addition, funds have been budgeted for the construction of an air strip at Grand Manan, at an estimated cost of $1 million.
Improvements to airports in Newfoundland and Labrador also are part of this program, with a total of $10.8 million allocated for Wabush, which is in my riding. A new air terminal and operations building is being built at Wabush, as well as a maintenance garage, fire hall, aircraft parking ramp, taxiway, air cargo site, parking lot and access road. In 1978 airstrips will be at Nain and Makkovik on the Labrador coast, at a total cost of $1 million for each site. Studies are under way for similar facilities at Marys Harbour and Hopedale. Also there is a master plan for 13 airstrips along the Labrador coast, which will revolutionize transportation in that eastern extremity of Canada. With that airstrip pattern, we will be able to institute a Twin Otter service, or perhaps a Dash-7 service. That will revolutionize transportation in that area.
The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte referred to the good old days when things could be transferred from the east to the west. The government has been studying the Maritime
April 25, 1978

Freight Rates Act and the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act which cover the Atlantic region and the Gaspe coast. Following consultation with the provincial governments, the government determined that existing subsidy for movements within the region did not provide the maximum possible economic benefit for the region, and in turn agreed a subsidy should be paid on selected regionally produced goods moving on all means of transportation. There will be a subsidy on selected goods manufactured and processed within the Atlantic area. The subsidy will not apply to those goods which come from other parts of Canada to be processed in the east and shipped back out again. The hon. member for Carleton-Char-lotte said that the rates are higher coming from Thunder Bay to New Brunswick. So what? It is a chance for the people in New Brunswick to produce their own goods and to become self-sufficient. I do not see that being a bad thing. We are changing the freight rate pattern and the levels of freight rates in Atlantic Canada in the interests of Atlantic Canada.
This subsidy will be implemented by September 1 on a selected list of commodities worked out by federal and provincial officials. I am convinced the revisions to the blanket 15 per cent subsidy program will have a positive economic effect on the entire region by making goods produced in Atlantic Canada more competitive and by improving competition in various forms of transportation.
Another program which affects all four Atlantic provinces is the urban transportation assistance program. It was designed to tackle a number of transportation problems affecting major cities. Each province would receive an amount for urban transportation projects which require attention. In the Atlantic region, New Brunswick will receive $6.8 million; Nova Scotia, $8.2 million; Newfoundland, $5.6 million; and Prince Edward Island, $1.2 million. As a result of these programs, I hope areas in my constituency, such as Grand Falls and Windsor, are provided with much needed arterial roads for the expansion of industrial parks and housing areas.
The province of Newfoundland has special transportation difficulties. In an attempt to solve them, the government formed a commission of inquiry to assess a wide range of factors affecting present and future transportation needs. I mention that in the beginning, because the Hall commission was referred to and the Sullivan commission was not mentioned. I draw the attention of hon. members opposite to that commission. The commission is charged with studying economic, social and geographic conditions in Newfoundland. It will provide us with an excellent framework through which we can work with the provincial government to achieve the best possible transportation system for that province. In other words, we are rationalizing transportation.
Marine coastal service has been subsidized over the years to the tune of tens of millions of dollars. The same amount of money can be put into transportation, a variety of modes, so that transportation in that province will be rationalized. The Sullivan commission has just about finished its work. Either the minister has a copy of its report in his possession or he will
Transportation
be provided with one soon. It will provide us with a policy line for the future of Newfoundland.
Also the government has been investigating the distribution system for potatoes from New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Working with provincial governments, potato producers and distributors, some significant improvements to the distribution system have been made, including revisions to potato freight rates, some improvements to port facilities in several places in Atlantic Canada, and a new operational planning system.
An important segment of the economy of Atlantic Canada centres around the shipbuilding industry. I am sure the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte will be interested in knowing that there are several projects which could mean a significant boost if a shipyard is the successful bidder. The design and construction of a hybrid nuclear gas-turbine polar icebreaker has been estimated at $310 million. If hydro-carbon development in the high Arctic continues, there is little doubt the government will need a polar icebreaker by the early 1980's. We hope that construction can be done in Atlantic Canada. We do not want absolute guarantees, but we do want to compete on a fair basis and we are hoping that that work can be done in a shipyard in Atlantic Canada.
Apart from the government's general programs, it has begun a number of specific improvements to transportation facilities throughout Atlantic Canada that will have a significant effect on both passenger and freight transportation in the area. For example, one project is the building of a new container handling terminal in Fairview Cove off Halifax harbour at a cost to the federal government of $2.1 million. The construction of this facility is already providing additional employment in the area, and following completion in 1980 more than 100 jobs will be created to operate the facility. The significant project in Prince Edward Island is the redevelopment of the Charlottetown airport to include a new terminal building, maintenance garage, fire hall and eventually a new 5,000 foot runway. This project, developed in consultation with provincial and municipal authorities, will cost more than $21 million, and work is expected to begin in the summer of 1978.
Oh, oh!

They do not want to hear the facts, Mr. Speaker. They do not want the record set straight; they only want to preach doom and gloom.
Other improvements at Charlottetown airport include a new maintenance garage, aircraft apron, carpark, access road system and taxiways. Gander airport in Newfoundland will also be receiving a new air control centre, expansion of its air terminal building and improvements to the north runway. The complete project will cost $18 million, and that is in addition to the movement by the federal government of the search and rescue centre to Gander, which is not only providing facilities and protection for our fishermen, but employment for people in Gander.

April 25, 1978
Transportation
Let me go on with the record.
It must be election time.

This is not going to do any harm for the election either.
The construction of one shed of the forest products terminal in Saint John, New Brunswick, was completed last year, and an additional shed will be completed shortly at a cost of $3.5 million. This new terminal is a major improvement in the handling of forest products at the port since they were previously handled at a number of diverse harbour facilities. The new specialized terminal ensures more efficient handling of all forest products, a major export of the province.
Although there is no funding involved, a major step towards streamlining the management of east coast ferry and coastal service was taken in December with the establishment of CN Marine, based in Moncton. The new corporation will function as a subsidiary to Canadian National Railways to provide incentives for efficient ferry operation, and help to control costing and deficits in providing these services. The previous method of offsetting operations deficits with federal funding created an ineffective management system and provided no incentives for operating efficiently. This new arrangement in no way diminishes the federal government's constitutional obligations, nor its responsibility for maintaining levels of service for those vital shipping links. We will continue to control rate setting and all major decisions affecting the services.
In addition to that movement of the centre of operation of east coast marine, new ferry services have been instituted in the Atlantic area. In my own riding, for example, they received a $500,000 subsidy last year to provide a new service across the Strait of Belle Isle between Newfoundland and Quebec and southern Labrador. There was an announcement just a week ago on the Sir Robert Bond
What have you done for the west coast?
Listen; just pay attention to the facts.
What about the ferries in B.C.?

There was a $4 million grant for the conversion of the Sir Robert Bond which links Louisport with Labrador. There has been a new truck carrying ferry inaugurated between Yarmouth, Nova Scotia and New England in addition to the Bluenose on that run.
These are substantial ferry improvements in eastern Canada and just some of the examples that this government has been concerned with, illustrating the fact that it has been doing something.
What did you do on the west coast?
What about the unemployment rate?
Order, please. The rules state that a member should be entitled to speak without interruption. I suggest we listen.
Hear, hear!

I welcome the interruptions, Mr. Speaker, from across the way because it shows their frame of mind. They do not have any real facts to put on the table, but are simply shouting and bawling to make themselves heard.
The opposition is talking about federal government consultation. Two years ago the Department of Transport created a directive to establish sound lines of communication between the department, provincial governments and industry. With respect to liaison with the provinces, this directive provides an effective channel for consultation and communication and ensures that the provincial point of view on transportation issues is known and understood by Transport Canada policymakers and given an objective and fair hearing. There are mechanisms within the department that we have set up to ensure that the provinces are consulted. Apart from these mechanisms, the Minister of Transport has had adequate consultation with all four Atlantic provinces-
Take Newfoundland, for example.

With Newfoundland as well. Before bringing in his policies this minister consulted with his counterparts. The record of this government in Atlantic Canada is clear, and the record of this Minister of Transport is also clear. Members on this side of the House from Atlantic Canada will agree with me that this is a minister that has been responsive and responsible.
When the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte says that policies are made by somebody pulled out of the PMO who has to go to work on transportation in Atlantic Canada, I want to inform him that we have had the Minister of Transport come to an Atlantic caucus. The improvements that have come about have been a result of this caucus. My caucus colleagues from Atlantic Canada will agree that this is one of the best ministers of transport that we have had, and certainly one that is-
Order, please. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a contribution to this most important debate initiated by my distinguished colleague from Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). I would like to put into proper perspective some of the things mentioned by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), particularly as they relate to western Canada. One thing that has really concerned and amazed me in this whole debate about transportation policy-particularly with a minister who comes from western Canada-is that when this minister is discussing the Hall commission report, which is so important to the future of western Canada and its buoyancy, I can come to no other conclusion than that he either has not
April 25, 1978

read the report, does not understand it, or cares not to understand it one whit.
I hope to demonstrate today by some of the points that I make that the minister completely misreads the importance of this particular commission report or completely misreads the very important and most germane portions of it.
He is trying to head it off.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
My colleague from Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) says that he is trying to head it off. One can come to no other conclusion except that the minister is in a position where he does not want to embrace the recommendations contained in this report and, in fact, is dragging his feet on some of the very important recommendations mentioned in it.
It has been pointed out on a number of occasions that of the recommendations made in the Hall commission report, there were something in the vicinity of-
Two recommendations.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
-six-I am being generous-of these recommendations which have been acted upon, notwithstanding the protestations of the minister. There are five others that have been partially acted upon but no action has been taken on the rest. The minister misunderstands the purport of the Hall commission report. He misunderstands this report which must be taken as a whole. Unless the recommendations are taken as such and implemented as a package, the results that are hoped to be gained from this particular report will not be attained.
It is interesting to see the minister's attitude toward this report. He takes a portion of it and indicates that he considers it the most important. He does not look at the report as a whole. Of the 92 recommendations he decides that number 91, say, is less important than number 90 and so on. In a letter to the Gravelbourg Star in Saskatchewan the minister indicated that he approached the report in that way when he wrote:
Since last May 16 when the Hall commission report was tabled in the House of Commons, the government has taken a swift but methodical approach to its implementation. On May 27 the most important recommendation in the Hall Report was implemented when some 1800 miles of prairie rail line was added to the basic network guaranteed to the year 2000.
The minister regards this report as one that merely deals either with the retention or the abandonment of rail lines in western Canada. That is a narrow approach. In his beneficence he announced, during the course of the debate, a number of very large grants for the improvement of rail lines in western Canada. Just after the report was presented the Western Producer carried the following report:
The elimination of some 2160 miles of branch line railways in Western Canada will save the Canadian taxpayers about $400 million annually, Chief Commissioner Emmett Hall told a May 16 press conference.
Referring to the minister's suggestion that the proposal for additional hopper cars would be a great asset to western Canada, the report went on:
Transportation
Regarding the federal government's proposal to build an additional 2000 grain hopper cars at a cost of $80 million, Mr. Hall said while these may be needed some time in future, they are only "make work" projects for Eastern industries and do not represent one additional dollar of revenue for Western Canada.
That is what Mr. Hall said about the minister's claims that he is paying great amounts of money to western Canada. Through rail line abandonment the government is saving something like S400 million annually, but the minister would suggest that he is giving about $100 million to western Canada for rail line improvement. People in western Canada understand what is happening, Mr. Speaker, and will not be fooled by such financial transactions. It has been pointed out that something like $55 million of that money will be spent in central Canada on rail and other supplies necessary for the improvement of rail lines.
I was somewhat amused during the debate when the minister accused the opposition of filibustering Bill C-33, introduced in his name. I think I should put some facts on the record with respect to that legislation. The minister said it was impossible to get the bill through because of the Conservative party. Mr. Speaker, I checked the record and I find that of seventeen speakers eight and a half were Liberals, two were NDP and six and a half were Conservatives. Hon. members may wonder about the two halves. One of the speakers was the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), so I apportioned one half of him to each side. If there was any filibustering I suggest the government should look within their own ranks.
The Minister of Transport said that Bill C-33 was a wonderful piece of legislation and would solve our national transportation problems. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce had other ideas, however, and I think it would be interesting to see what he said about it. Since the minister is not in the House tonight and there is no member present on the government side from western Canada, I shall put this on the record and they can read it tomorrow. I see the parliamentary secretary is here. Indeed, he is always here and does a good job. He stays in the House and listens.
The Minister of Transport thought this bill so important that he had the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) introduce it and read his speech. This was supposed to be an important breakthrough in transportation policy but that is what happened.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, then an ordinary member like the rest of us, chastised the Minister of Transport for not being in the chamber. At page 3530 of Hansard for March 1, 1977 he is reported as follows:
... he has lost favour with the Liberal backbenchers, so the government has demoted him and sent him out west because they do not want the backbenchers of the Liberal party to enter this debate, and they felt that if he was here initiating the debate he would antagonize his own members and provoke a discussion.
The Minister of Transport has accused us of holding up the bill and filibustering, but here is what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said a little later.
I believe that this legislation takes the government from the mess it was in and puts it in another mess.

April 25, 1978
Transportation
What words of commendation for this wonderful legislation that the Minister of Transport says is essential to the future of transportation in Canada!
I could go on and on Mr. Speaker, but I have underlined portions of the speech and would be glad to send it to any member of the government who wants to know what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce thought of Bill C-33. March 1977 was a critical period in his political life; that was when it became crystal clear to him that the time had come to accept a portfolio under the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I want to deal with the Hall commission report because it is so very important to western Canada, although in its ramifications it affects all of Canada. Because the grain handling system in western Canada is being improved, we tend to take it for granted that any assistance given or changes made will fill the pockets of western Canadians. Nothing could be further from the truth, Mr. Speaker. If we consider the importance of grain exports to the balance of trade and consider the amount of money spent on goods and equipment from other parts of Canada, we realize that the agricultural industry, and the grain industry in particular, must be seen as essential to the future well-being of the country.
The minister seems to think he is moving fast enough on the recommendations of the Hall commission. Although he pays lip service to those recommendations, only five have been implemented and there is ample evidence to suggest that the minister has no interest in the total package. I am sorry to report that the Minister of Transport has not approached Mr. Justice Hall or called him in since his report was presented to discuss the ramifications of it.
What a peculiar situation we are in. The minister said that we are going to go ahead with the report. But what they forgot to do was to ask the person who was the head of this important commission for his advice and interpretation of the recommendations contained in the commission's report. As I say, not once has the government got together with Mr. Justice Hall. Not once has the government sought an explanation or a clarification or asked him for his assistance in bringing forward meaningful implementation of this most important report.
What have the government done? They have set up what they call a Prairie Rail Action Committee. In Saskatoon we know what action committees are all about. It is a political motto used by the Minister of Transport. It is a convenient kind of spin-off between what has been going on politically on one side and what is going on now with this commission. We have some serious reservations with respect to this action committee. In my opinion the creation of this committee is merely another form of stall for the purpose of avoiding the implementation of these worth-while recommendations of the Hall commission. The effect of it will be to put the control of transportation and grain handling, in particular transportation,

back into the hands of the Canadian Transport Commission which is now a central and eastern dominated commission.
I want to briefly go over some of the points which must be taken in the total context as far as the Hall commission report is concerned. It has to be taken as a package. One recommendation cannot be isolated and expected to solve the whole problem. Concerning the grain handling system in western Canada there were something like 5,758 elevators in the prairie region in 1938. In 1976 the number of elevators had been reduced to about 3,964. The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, one of the largest grain elevator companies in western Canada, say that it is their intention to rationalize the number of elevators down to something like 550. There are presently just over 1,000. If elevators on a line are removed, then there is nothing left to justify retaining a railway in that particular area.
The Hall commission could not get specific information from the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool as to which elevators would be retained and which elevators would not be retained. As a result they recommended the creation of a prairie rail authority. The commission could see that some 2,000 miles of railway would have no grain to carry if these elevators were closed down. Therefore, they directed abandonment of roughly 1,800 miles. This left about 2,343 miles in doubt. The commission indicated that nothing could be done with respect to decisions on these lines until the grain companies had made up their minds regarding these elevators.
In his brief, Mr. Runciman of the United Grain Growers pointed out that decisions made in this connection in 1976 could be wrong in 1986. As I mentioned, the commission recommended a prairie rail authority. It was felt that money should be spent to keep these doubtful lines operational, but that no money should be spent to upgrade them.
I suggest to you, sir, that the government has ignored the recommendations of the commission in setting up this Prairie Rail Action Committee. It has been stated by my colleagues on this side, the hon. member for Vegreville and the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), that the concept of a western component of the CTC should be kept alive and should be implemented. Notwithstanding the statements of the government that they would do this at some time, I suggest it is something which should be looked at as an immediate priority. The decisions that will be made by the Prairie Rail Action Committee will be made before decisions are made by grain companies as to which elevators will be abandoned. This, I suggest to you, sir, could result in very high costs to the country.
It is also important to understand in terms of western Canada, central Canada and so on, that central Canada benefits from the grain industry and derives substantial benefits with respect to the price paid for grain, flour and ultimately bread. The commission has pointed out that eastern millers get the benefit of the Crow rate which is so often attacked and which was brought into question by none other than the Minister of Transport on a number of occasions. Wheat is stored along the seaway. With western grain produc-
April 25, 1978

ers-that is, the Canadian Wheat Board-paying, storage charges were originally one-thirtieth of a cent per day and 1 believe it has now been moved up to one-twentieth of a cent per day. This is paid for out of the pockets of the western farmer. There is no question that the Minister of Transport and this government have abandoned the prairie rail authority concept by having named the Prairie Rail Action Committee-
Order, please. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been waiting for a long time for this opposition day on the transportation policy in Canada. I was naive enough to believe that opposition members might suggest some measures and concrete solutions to the admittedly important problems we must face when drawing up a national policy in this very important area of our economy and the life of this country, because that policy has an impact on national unity.
So, Mr. Speaker, I admit that I am very disappointed, after listening to this debate from the start, to have heard for hours on end all about what the government failed to do, that the transportation policy should provide for advisory groups with the provinces, that it should be based or oriented toward a better economic development of Canada, that there should be a western arm, and an eastern arm of the Canadian Transport Commission, when all those points, Mr. Speaker, were made repeatedly by the government, and more particularly in the 1975 transportation policy statement.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to deal more specifically with the achievements in the area of transportation, particularly in the province of Quebec. During this debate and in previous ones, we did not often have the opportunity to hear from members opposite about what is being done by Transport Canada in Quebec. Every time they deal with transportation issues pertaining to the province, all they can say is that the government is spending too much money in Mirabel, that freight rates in the province of Quebec are too favourable in relation with the rates in the Maritimes, or that the aircraft maintenance facilities in Dorval should be moved to Toronto.
I am aware that our hon. friends opposite are sadly lacking as far as their representation in the province of Quebec is concerned, and that is why I am so glad, Mr. Speaker, to be able to enlighten them a little about the great accomplishments of Transport Canada in that province.
Most hon. members opposite have complained with a lot of energy and concern about the great problems we are facing in the rail passenger service in Canada. Unfortunately all of them have touched very lightly on this great achievement of this government, namely the creation of VIA Rail. And 1 should like to deal briefly about this new Crown corporation which is
Transportation
especially beneficial to the province of Quebec. Everyone knows that historically railways originated in the Montreal area and that Montreal is also the site of Canadian National and Canadian Pacific head offices, therefore it was only logical in my opinion that the headquarters of VIA Rail should be located in Montreal as they have been.
Mr. Speaker, it will be recalled that in 1967, under the National Transportation Act, the government had committed itself to pay 80 per cent of passenger service deficits of both railways, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. It became obvious in 1974 that that policy had fallen short of the expected results for there was a SI67 million deficit and the projected deficit for 1980 would have reached $400 million. So in 1977 the government decided to set up a new corporation called VIA Rail and to merge the services of both the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways in order to give a boost to that important mode of transportation.
Mr. Speaker, the challenge faced by VIA Rail is to establish an efficient passenger rail transportation system at reasonable cost. They must also aim at a significant reduction of the subsidy and launch an innovative marketing program to regain public trust in this means of transportation. We are convinced that the income will increase in the long term. Of course they are not expected to report profits in the first years of operation, but I am quite confident in the management and in the chairman of VIA Rail who I know are all doing their best so this new service will earn the share of the Canadian market it deserves in the field of transportation.
In order to allay the concern of our friends of the New Democratic Party who often complain that we tried to deprive Canadians of services for the sake of profit, they must be reminded that in the terms of reference of VIA Rail as in the legislation passed last fall on Air Canada-and this also applies to the CN bill we are now examining-in each of those acts there is always a provision allowing the government to decide that, in a given underdeveloped area of the country that is either underpopulated or lacks a good industrial infrastructure, a service can continue to be given through government subsidies whether it be passager trains, air service or freight trains.
Mr. Speaker, as we know also, in order to help VIA Rail, Transport Canada has entrusted a Montreal company, after calling for tenders right across the land, of course, with the care of redecorating passenger cars that will be transferred by the CP to the CN. Those cars will first be used on the lines running in the Quebec City-Windsor corridor and on the continental run and allow passengers to travel by train in greater comfort. The minister has also asked the Montreal company, Bombardier M.L.W., to build ten LRC trains; that new material will include 22 locomotives and 50 cars bought jointly by the federal government and VIA Rail at an approximate cost of $90 million.

April 25, 1978
Transportation
Mr. Speaker, I feel all hon. members must rejoice in the fact that a Montreal company managed to get that contract; when those new trains go into service in 1980, we will prove to the whole world how technologically advanced we are in the field of railway transport, which will surely help us export and sell Quebec and Canadian technology in world markets.
This $90 million project will create 1,500 man-years of employment over a three-year period. Many Canadian companies, including Alcan and Dofasco, are partly responsible for developing this new LRC train and will be the main suppliers of Bombardier M.L.W., which means Mr. Speaker, and this should be emphasized, that the Canadian content as concerns manpower, material and engineering will be 80 per cent for the engines and 96 per cent for the cars.
Still in the railway field, Mr. Speaker, MOT has just purchased 488 cars for moving grain at a cost of $18.5 million from Marine Industries Ltd. of Sorel, and these will be added to the 150 other cars which are now being manufactured at a cost of $6 million under the Prairie branch line rehabilitation program. By the way, Mr. Speaker, I would like to note that while the previous speaker complained about the government's delay in implementing the recommendations of the Hall report, he should remember, as one of my colleagues on this side of the House said earlier, that 11 days after the publication of this report, about 1,800 miles of lines were transferred to the basic railway network of western Canada, and that since then, we have spent $175 million to rehabilitate the lines and that the government is also committed to an eight-year program to rehabilitate all western lines at an approximate cost of $600 million. This is not doing nothing, Mr. Speaker, and I feel that we should not worry but rather keep going in this direction, because I believe that our transportation policy is very useful to all Canadians, both from eastern and western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, after speaking briefly about railways, I should now like to go on to another area, that of the automobile. I am happy to note that the work done at the car testing center in Blainville which has cost us $20 million will soon be completed. The center will provide various tests this summer. It will undertake research and investigations on the defects and the compliance to Canadian standards of the various car models. This center will also make its equipment available to the government, private industry and private research organisations. There is another area, Mr. Speaker, where great progress was made by MOT in 1977 in Quebec, namely shipping. I should like to recall briefly the extensive investments made in Montreal harbour which have already started and the announcement made during a cabinet meeting held in Montreal last December, namely that the government will try to develop Montreal harbour so as to increase considerably the handling of containers which is important for our economy, and to give a new economic impetus to the Montreal area by

creating new jobs there. The National Harbours Board will invest $37.5 million in this project. One of the aspects of the project is the upgrading of the Racine container terminal, at a cost of $26 million, which will be of tremendous benefit to the economy of the Montreal area.
Along the same lines, Mr. Speaker, this terminal will create 80 permanent jobs and 500 man-years of employment in the four years of construction work. The other group of projects concerns the $11.5 million program for the upgrading of grain elevators. This amount does not include the demolition of centres 1 and 2 but it covers the old harbour modernization project and provides for the automation of weighing facilities and for the improvement of both the electrical system and the grain-loading facilities for trucks at elevator No. 3. Other changes will be made under the form of interconnected galleries and so on, at elevators No. 4 and 5. Those extensive works, Mr. Speaker, will enable Montreal harbour to maintain its strategic and competitive position and to continue to serve efficiently the agricultural food industry in Quebec and the Canadian export market.
Mr. Speaker, another harbour where we have tried to improve conditions is obviously the Quebec City harbour where, under a federal project of $42 million to refit the old harbour, an amount of $8 million will be allotted to the reconstruction of piers along the shores of the St. Lawrence, that is piers 21 to 8 and their extension up to the western limit of the federal property. Those works will provide 300 jobs and will accommodate visiting ships as well as freighters at anchor. Also in the Quebec harbour, Mr. Speaker, the Department of Transport has approved an investment of $3 million for the renovation of a grain elevator. That elevator is owned by the National Harbours Board and has been rented to Bunge of Canada Limited since 1967. This company will provide the other $6 million required to carry out this program. Again in the Quebec City area, Mr. Speaker, the National Harbours Board is working in co-operation with l'Administration du port de Quebec on a development plan that would create an industrial harbour zone on the sandbanks of Beauport. Their objectives are the following: minimize the development costs, provide functional and harmoniously integrated development and finally secure the development of management techniques suited to the efficient application of such a plan. The Beauport sandbanks cover approximately 1,065 acres, including 450 mainly from embankments made up from the dredging of the river.
We have also discussed at length, Mr. Speaker, the adverse effects that the move of CP Navigation will have on Quebec harbour. To offset this loss of tonnage, Quebec harbour authorities joined with l'Association des producteurs de bois de sciage and the province of Quebec to carry out an important study of the viability of a forest product terminal in Quebec City. This study will deal with transport, distribution, marketing and organization of that undertaking. The cost of the
April 25, 1978

study, that is some $73,000, will be shared by the three parties involved and we expect the study to be published by late May or early June.
I could give many more examples of investments, such as the $3 million invested in the Chicoutimi dock to make it a tanker dock open to ships carrying oil products for the Saguenay region. I could also refer to a plan for improving the use of Trois-Rivieres harbour, but I could not leave unmentioned the $12.5 million investment at Gros-Cacouna for the establishment of a general cargo harbour. Also, Mr. Speaker, as concerns Sept-Iles, the second most important harbour in Canada, the department will soon publish a long range development plan which will give this harbour the tools necessary for its development. It will therefore be necessary to develop an implementation strategy as soon as possible. The provincial and municipal authorities have already recognized the importance of Sept-Iles harbour and of its development, and are willing to offer us all the support necessary for its achievement.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are some of our achievements in the maritime field in Quebec for 1977. I did not want to go back to 1974 or 1970, for fear of frightening my colleagues opposite. Despite all these investments in 1977, there are others to be made, and the minister himself as well as his officials are conscious of the fact that maritime development is a major asset in the economy of Quebec which is the door to the rest of Canada. As far as other future projects are concerned, and which are under consideration at the moment, I think we must look into regional development, for example the development of a harbour in Pointe-au-Pic, in Charlevoix county, which would complement the harbours in Quebec City and Baie-Comeau which serve a more important purpose.
In the few minutes I have left, Mr. Speaker, I also wish to refer briefly to air transportation. I should mention that in 1975-76, 13,000 people in Quebec were working in air transportation in the private sector or in the public sector. And this excludes employees working for provincial or municipal governments or for local carriers. In addition to that direct effect on employment, the air transportation industry has significant economic fall-outs in distribution and manufacturing throughout Quebec. Suffice to recall the production by Canadair of the Challenger aircraft which is one of the outstanding achievements of modern aviation on international markets. Or again the numerous contracts awarded to the firm Pratt and Whitney to meet the requirements of the Department of National Defence; in its Quebec plant that firm will receive $140 million in Department of National Defence contracts out of a total of $250 million.
In October 1976, the federal government authorized Canadair to build a total of 250 Challenger aircraft which represent, Mr. Speaker, an injection of $1.2 billion into the economy of the province of Quebec. To date, 120 aircraft have been
Transportation
sold which represents an inflow of $600 million. The total number of employment created only by that aircraft is 1,900.
As concerns airport facilities, everybody knows that Montreal has two major airports, Mirabel and Dorval. We are now studying a development plan for Mirabel airport that should be implemented at the beginning of 1980. This plan will include the development of Dorval airport. I shall not mention the many investments in air transportation at Sept-Iles, Mont-Joli and Quebec City, but there is still much to do in that field and within a limited budget, we are still working to find answers to the problems of the people in Magdalen Islands, Gaspe, Bonaventure, Havre-Saint-Pierre and other communities.
So, Mr. Speaker, I insisted on mentioning a few figures and a few accomplishments to make it clear that the motion introduced by hon. members opposite has no ground whatsoever when you compare the unfounded statements it contains with the facts and the achievements of Transport Canada.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of his speech, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lapointe) said he hoped to hear positive suggestions from this side of the House. From what he said, it is obvious he would not acknowledge a positive suggestion coming from the opposition, because the contributions of opposition members did contain a great many positive proposals in the area of transport. I will do the same, although with some concern I must admit, because this government is well known and famous throughout Canada for their policy which is to borrow ideas from the opposition. Government members just might appropriate the ideas I will submit tonight and convert them into electoral promises.

Because, after all, they were only electoral promises. Some may have noticed how many of the projects contained in that long catalogue recited by the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) were cast in the future tense-the government was about to do this or that; it was about to build a road up into Labrador, it was about to do something at Wabush. Why, after ten years, has the government decided so late in the day to put forward this enormous catalogue? Why did it decide to wait until now before bringing these proposals forward? All it was, was a catalogue of goodies, an attempt to get votes.
Indeed, I was afraid, when my hon. friend from Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) was referring to certain aspects of the need for reform in prairie transportation policies, that the government would be prompted to issue still more election promises between now and election day. I say, let Canadians beware.

April 25, 1978
Transportation
I do not remember too much Latin, but there is one thing I do remember. I will not say it in Latin, but the English translation is: "I fear the Greeks when they come with gifts in their hands". I would like to update that quotation from Virgil. I think it should read like this, and I put it in the exhortative: "Mistrust the Liberals, especially when they come with gifts on their tongues". With all these misgivings I intend to take a risk and deal with a problem on which an election promise might very well be made. I will just have to take the risk, but once again I go back to that old expression which we see so often, and I will translate that to the occasion and say, "Cave, Canada,"-"beware, Canada". I will come back to that.
There are two problems about which I would like to speak tonight. One of them has to do with a railroad on Vancouver Island which has a long history of being shut down by the Canadian Transport Commission, started up again and shortened, and I think it may very well be lengthened. I suppose it goes back to 1905 when a grant was made to the CPR or to another company to establish a railway between Esquimalt and Nanaimo.
The E and N Railway had been in service in one form or another running from Esquimalt right up to Courtenay, and for some reason there was an interruption. The CPR claimed it would not be able to carry on the service any longer, and it asked if it could be discharged of its responsibility to run that particular service. Hearings were called by the CTC in Victoria. I, for one, made a submission to that hearing on March 8, 1976.
I had a variety of reasons for arguing against the closing of that particular service. My first reason for opposing the CPR petition stemmed from the legal obligation accepted by the CPR when it applied in the first instance to operate the railway, which it was prepared to accept in return for proprietary rights and a substantial grant of land by the Crown amounting to 1.9 million acres. That was what the CPR was granted in return for building and operating the railway. I thought that was a sufficient argument for it to go on operating the railway. It was supplemented, actually, by a rather philosophic argument connected with the relationship between the acceptance of a privilege, that is, the right to make use of the 1.9 million acres, and the performance of a service undertaken as a result of that acceptance.
There was a variety of other reasons which I brought forward, and I submitted them to the Railway Transport Committee. That was on March 8, 1976, and in July, the Railway Transport Committee ordered that the CPR reconstruct two bridges located at certain mileages in accordance with an annexed order, and so on. That was promptly done. The date of that order was July 28, 1976.
Then came the next step in the proceedings. The CPR finished the job. It built the bridges and prepared the railway for operation. Then, having heard from the CPR that in the year 1972 there was a loss attributable to the operations of the passenger train service of the order $176,000, in 1973, $190,-
[Mr. Munro (Esquimalt-Saanich).l
000 and in 1974, $231,000, the Canadian Transport Commission ordered that, as of January 31, 1978, the CPR should discontinue the operation of the passenger train service, having previously instructed the CPR to build bridges and put the railway back into operating condition.
That, of course, was quite an extraordinary order. Freight was being transported on that line twice a week. It was carried throughout the whole service, but the transport of passengers was to cease. That caused the province of British Columbia to give notice that it was going to appeal that ruling. A letter to that effect was sent on December 27, 1977 to the chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission.
I too felt that that was not quite the way things should be, but with a little bit of pressure from the provincial government and letters from a variety of people, including several members of parliament from that part of the country, we managed, on January 20, 1978, to get the CTC to agree that the date should be changed to June 30. We are fast approaching June 30. June 30 may be a very important date, and this is why I have some fear about the conversion of this suggestion into an electoral promise, but there has been more pressure built up suggesting that this railway is required. The Regional District of Greater Victoria, for example, submitted a telegram to the CTC on January 18, 1978 indicating that the railway should continue. I too argued for that.
I was not aware yesterday when I was working in my office that I would be taking part in this debate, but I received a submission from one of my constituents, and last night I dictated a letter which I sent to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), a copy of which was sent to the chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission, arguing that the June 30 date should be erased from the record and that the CPR should be ordered to maintain the service through the summer months until there is opportunity to have another look at this matter. I have this letter in front of me now.
I was puzzled as to why June 30 should be chosen as the date to close the railway. June 30 is just the beginning of the tourist season.
Election.
I do not think it was known back in January when the extension to June 30 was discussed that there might be an election in or around June, but it is beginning to smell a little bit like that now.
They still don't know.

That is true.
One of the arguments I advanced then-and I advance it again now-is that the timetable for the running of this particular railway should be more in tune with the needs of the communities up island so that people can come down to Victoria and go back on the same day. People from Victoria who wish to have a day's outing on the railway are able to leave in the morning and come back in the evening. That is not the way it works for people up island. The train leaves from
April 25, 1978

Victoria and comes back to Victoria at night so that people up island have to stay in Victoria overnight and go back the following morning.
As I have said, there is some danger that between now and election day a promise will be made that an order will go out to the Canadian Transport Commission to continue this service at least through the summer months. If that happens, I think that by now the Canadian public will be aware that it is an election promise and will look at it for what it is worth.
One other matter that could well become an election promise-because the Minister of Transport has been reminded of it often enough within the last three or four weeks or months- is the provision of radar at Victoria International Airport. I remember when I raised this question that I spoke of the incident which really prompted the question. It was on January 21, 1977, and I made a note about seeing an aircraft go by the port windows as we made a swift bank to starboard. I looked into the matter and found out what had happened.
There are a few statistics here which I think are worth putting on the record to indicate the place of Victoria International Airport among other airports across Canada. I will give the rank of these airports according to the traffic using the airport. I will be happy to see this information on the record.
In fifth rank is Vancouver International Airport. In 1977 there were 235,825 flights in and out of the airport. Edmonton is eighth in rank with 231,060. Calgary is ninth, with 208,170. Victoria is thirteenth with 178,707. Then I will mention two important and interesting ones. Number 16 is Dorval International with 159,361, as compared with Victoria which has 178,707 flights. I have a funny feeling in the pit of my stomach that there is radar at the Dorval International Airport but there is not at Victoria. I would like to bet that there is not a member in the House who could guess where Mirabel ranks on the list of airports used. It is forty-seventh, with 50,447 flights a year.
That is not so.
Mais si. This is the report here.
Which year?

Gander is fifty-fifth in rank with 36,686 flights. I have a reason for making this selection. I suspect that Edmonton and Calgary both have radar. I do not know for sure, but I suspect they do because I am always being told that the traffic coming into Victoria is being directed from Vancouver. What about Dorval and Mirabel? Are hon. members going to suggest that only Dorval or only Mirabel has radar? Mirabel needs it to bring aircraft in from overseas, I agree, but does it control the traffic to Dorval as well?
I would like to mention why I have picked Gander as No. 55 with only 36,686 flights, about 3,000 a month. The old radar
Transportation
that was taken out of Vancouver airport was hurriedly put on a train and shipped out to Gander so that there could not be a movement afoot in Victoria to have it shipped 80 miles across the water and mounted at Victoria International Airport.
The figures I mentioned are impressive and I do not need to repeat them. They will appear in tomorrow's Hansard and they can be checked and rechecked against the statistics put out in the annual report of aircraft movements by Transport Canada. It is simple and straightforward.
I warn everybody that if a promise is made between now and election day that radar will be placed in Victoria International Airport, we will all be grateful but we will know why it is being done.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words in this special debate on transportation because those of us who live in northern Ontario have suffered from the inadequacy of every national transportation policy that this Liberal government has designed.
I have made speeches in the past outlining the concerns of those of us in the north about the need for a rational transportation policy. I do not have time to go into that again this evening, but I would like to reiterate our concern that if we allow the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to implement fully his concept of profit oriented and user-pay modes of transport to override the concept of service, then in areas of sparse population, such as northern Ontario and elsewhere in Canada, we will suffer because we just do not have the population or the usage on the various modes of transport to make them always pay their own way. Surely if we are serious about national unity, service at times must come before profit.
We in northern Ontario know what it is to have discriminatory freight rates, how this has inhibited the development of secondary manufacturing in our part of the province and how it has perpetuated the export of resources because it is always cheaper to ship out the nickel, the iron ore or the pulp and paper than to have them processed, developed and manufactured in northern Ontario. Until we solve the transportation freight rate problem, we are not going to solve the problem of unemployment. Only by developing manufacturing industry will we be able to provide jobs for young people living in northern Ontario.
I do not want to go into details on that aspect because I have talked about it in the past. What I would like to focus on is some discriminatory policies of this government as they affect my constituency of Sault Ste. Marie. We have witnessed over the past decade or so, as I have said, discrimination in terms of the freight rate policy on rail, lack of air service and bad highways and roads. But recently, under the present Minister of Transport, we have suffered another blow, in fact two blows, the first being the ending of the passenger rail service between Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury in the name of economy. This government, which subsidized passenger rail service, decided that it could save some money by ending that subsidy, and therefore the CTC was allowed to let CPR discontinue

April 25, 1978
Transportation
that passenger rail service. Many communities along that route suffered, making the transportation problem even harder. People were forced to rely on buses and other modes of transport, to the detriment of their travel schedules.
That was the first blow that we received only about a year and a half ago. More recently, in fact a couple of weeks ago, the Minister of Transport dealt us another blow by announcing a cut-back in the operation of the ship canal or lock at Sault Ste. Marie. We have only one Canadian lock to bring vessels from Lake Superior to the lower Great Lakes. The rest of the locks are owned by the United States. Our lock was an old one that had not been upgraded or enlarged over the years and was indeed allowed to deteriorate.
The first rumour was that the government was going to close the lock at Sault Ste. Marie by 1982. It was based on the erroneous argument that the lock was no longer commercially viable, that tonnage was being reduced, and therefore, the government could not afford the $1 million annual expenditure to keep the lock open. Representations were made by myself, the union involved, the city council of Sault Ste. Marie and the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). Our arguments were in favour of increasing the usage of the lock by upgrading and indeed building a larger lock. Those arguments fell on deaf ears.
I should like to examine the minister's argument in favour of cutting back the service provided by the lock. He has cut out the night shift, which means the lock no longer operates on a 24-hour basis. The inevitable result of that is a reduction of the tonnage going through that lock. Thus, this time next year the Minister of Transport will be in a position to produce figures indicating that the tonnage is down even more, and that therefore the lock is not commercially viable and must be closed.
When the announcement was first made regarding the closure of that lock, I made immediate representations to the minister as to why I felt the lock should remain open and indeed should be improved. The Minister of Transport sent a letter to me dated February 15, 1978, dealing with the prospect for growth in traffic and whether the lock should remain open. In part the letter reads as follows:
Nevertheless, when I look at projections of traffic through the Canadian-Ameri-can lock system at Sault Ste. Marie, I note that no capacity problems are envisaged until some time after 1995. In these times of financial restraint for the federal government, I am doubtful that there would be much merit in Transport Canada undertaking a cost-benefit analysis of a new super lock, since there would be very few benefits in terms of a more efficient transportation system until after that date.
The minister has erred by not doing a cost-benefit analysis. He has not taken into account some recent developments. That is the reason I appeal to the Minister of Transport to reconsider his argument that he does not foresee any problems concerning growth in the system and the need for building a new and larger lock at Sault Ste. Marie.
The minister has not taken into account some recent figures concerning projected coal shipments from western Canada to
[Mr. Symes.l
Thunder Bay, and then through the St. Lawrence seaway system, in order to fulfil Ontario Hydro contracts. By 1980, 3.9 million tons of coal will be delivered annually to Thunder Bay, and then trans-shipped by water to various points in the Great Lakes. That represents a 12 per cent increase in total Canadian coal production. It means that increased tonnage will go through that lock system, carrying coal to various parts of Canada. In light of that increased tonnage projection, there is a strong argument in favour of that lock's hours of operation not being reduced. The 24 hour operation should be maintained, and indeed the size of the lock should be expanded, or a new one should be built.
This would ensure a Canadian presence and a Canadian option at this important junction in the Great Lakes. Of course, that is important in terms of future bargaining on the seaway, but also it would help our failing shipping industry. New vessels will have to be built to trans-ship the coal. They will be larger vessels. Thus, the expansion of the lock would encourage the Canadian shipbuilding industry to make use of this new movement of goods.
Also I am discouraged that the federal government has not taken into account, aside from the need for a Canadian presence at the lock and the need for a fully operative lock at that point, the fact that this lock provides annually an infusion of $1 million into the local economy of Sault Ste. Marie in terms of wages, repair work and other contracts let in conjunction with the operation of the lock. That is not an insignificant sum, especially considering the repressed state of much of the economy in northern Ontario.
As an alternative, the minister proposes building an historic park in the area and infusing $170,000 a year for the maintenance of that park. That falls far short of the revenues which would be generated locally by maintaining the full operation of the lock. We should not be backed into an "either/or" situation. An historic park in the area is compatible with a full-time commercial operation of the lock. Indeed, it is important for our tourist industry. Some 80,000 visitors are attracted each year to the lock to watch its operations. The Americans attract over one million visitors a year who view the operations of their lock. The reason the Americans are able to attract more people is because larger vessels can be handled by their lock. By upgrading our lock, a shot in the arm would be given to the tourist industry in the area.
Also I am disturbed by the information which the minister has been given by officials in his department concerning the actual tonnage going through the lock. His figures indicate that in 1972, 1,120,570 tons went through the lock; by 1976 it had declined to 564,350 tons. The figures I have obtained from the union involved, which are the figures of the lock itself, indicate that in 1972 the tonnage was 1,523,754; in 1976, 1,288,903; and declining in 1977 to 709,890 tons.
Those figures are very different from the figures of the minister. They do not indicate as dramatic a drop as his figures do. The factor which has not been taken into account, as far as the drop in 1977 is concerned, is the summer-long strike in 1977 of the iron mining industry in Minnesota. Also,
April 25, 1978

the fact that the average water level on that system of the lakes had dropped from 20 feet to 17 feet 10 inches was not taken into account. That prohibited many ships from making use of the facility.
We cannot allow the kind of discrimination practised by this minister to continue. That system is important to Sault Ste. Marie. The workers want to continue working there under the jurisdiction of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. I appeal to the minister to reconsider this very regressive decision.
